(p-53)(Surat al-Anbiya' is Meccan, and its verses number one hundred and twelve.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Their reckoning has drawn near for people.﴾

The connection (munasabah, the thematic link between passages) of this noble opening to the noble closing verses before it is too clear to need explanation. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "By 'people' is meant the polytheists, and this is what the following verses make clear. By 'the drawing near of their reckoning' is meant its drawing near within the drawing near of the Hour. The attribution of the drawing near to the reckoning, and not to the Hour, although the Hour entails it and all the other terrifying events and states within it, is because the discourse is directed toward explaining their heedlessness of it and their turning away from what reminds them of it. The preposition 'li' (for) is connected to the verb, and its placement before the subject is to hasten the infusion of awe, for attributing the drawing near to them from the outset is something that distresses them, brings them dread, and unsettles them with regard to what is drawing near. Likewise, the placement of the prepositional phrase before the direct object in His words, ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾, is to hasten the delight, since stating that creation was for the sake of the addressees is something that gladdens them and increases their desire for what was created for them and their longing for it. He also made it an emphasis on the addition, on the basis that the customary original form among ordinary speakers would be 'the reckoning of people has drawn near,' then 'the reckoning has drawn near for people,' then 'the reckoning of them has drawn near for people'; yet this is a complete affectation, far removed from what the context requires. What the arrangement of the discourse calls for is what we have already mentioned. The meaning is: the reckoning of their evil deeds, which entail punishment, has come near to them. In attributing the drawing near, which indicates a turning toward them, to the reckoning, although it is possible to reverse this, so that the turning and approach are considered to come from them toward it, there is an exaltation of its status and a magnification of its matter that is not hidden, since it is depicted as a thing approaching them that continually pursues them and inevitably overtakes them. The meaning of its drawing near to them is that it draws close and approaches them after having been distant from them, for at every hour of time it is nearer to them than it was in the hour before. As for the excuse that its nearness is relative to the time that has passed, or relative to God, Mighty and Majestic, or on the ground that every coming thing is near, these have no bearing on what we are discussing of the drawing near derived from the form of the past tense, and there is no need for them in establishing the basic meaning. Yes, it may be understood from it, by custom, that it is near in itself as well, and then one proceeds to the first interpretation rather than the other two. As for the second, there is no way to consider it here, because its nearness relative to Him, exalted is He, is something in which renewal and variation cannot be conceived with certainty; its consideration appears only in His words, ﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ and similar expressions, which do not indicate occurrence. As for the third, it contains no indication of nearness in the real sense, even relative to something else."

﴿And they are in heedlessness﴾: that is, in complete heedlessness of it, utterly unmindful of it, not merely that they are unconcerned about it while acknowledging its coming. Rather, they deny it and disbelieve in it, even though their intellects require that deeds must have a recompense.

﴿Turning away﴾: that is, from the signs and warnings that alert them out of the slumber of heedlessness. These two are predicates of the pronoun. Since heedlessness was a natural condition for them, the first predicate was made a prepositional phrase, indicating stability, in contrast to turning away. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "people." It has also been permitted that the prepositional phrase be a circumstantial clause relating to the concealed pronoun in "turning away."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 2:

﴿There does not come to them any reminder﴾ — i.e., any portion sent down from the Qur'an that reminds them of it in the most complete manner and alerts them away from heedlessness with the most thorough alerting, as if it were the very essence of the Reminder (dhikr).

The "min" in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿from their Lord﴾ is for the initial point of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya), used figuratively, and it is connected either to ﴿comes to them﴾ or to an omitted element that is an attribute of "reminder." Whichever it is, it indicates the excellence and nobility of the Reminder and the complete heinousness of what they did to it. The mention of the title "Lord" (rububiyya) serves to intensify the reproach.

﴿Newly revealed﴾ (muhdath) is in the genitive case (bi-l-jarr) as an attribute of "reminder." It has also been read in the nominative (bi-l-raf') by taking it as agreeing with its place (hamlan 'ala mahallihi), meaning: its sending down is newly made according to what wisdom requires.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿except that they listen to it﴾ are an exceptive clause of the defective type (istithna' mufarragh), whose place is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of "comes to them," with "qad" either implied or not, according to the well-known difference of opinion. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿while they play﴾ are a circumstantial clause from the subject of "listen to it."

And His saying, ﴿their hearts distracted﴾: it is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) following the previous one, or a *hal* relating to the waw in "يَلْعَبُونَ" (*yal'abūn*, "they play"). The meaning is: no fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord, in any state, except that they listen to it while playing, mocking it, and heedless of it, or playing with it, while their hearts are distracted from it, because of the extremity of their heedlessness and their excessive turning away from reflecting on matters and considering their consequences. It is also read "لاهِيَةٌ" (*lāhiyatun*, with a *ḍamma*), in which case it is a predicate following a predicate (*khabar ba'da khabar*).

﴿And they concealed their private conversation﴾: this is a new sentence (*kalām mustaʾnaf*), brought to specify their particular crimes, following the account of their customary crimes. "النَّجْوى" (*al-najwā*, "private conversation") is a noun from *tanājī* (confiding in one another secretly). The meaning of concealing it, although it can only be secret, is that they went to great lengths to hide it, or that they concealed the very act of conferring, such that no one perceived that they were conferring privately.

His saying, ﴿those who did wrong﴾: it is an apposition (*badal*) for the waw of "أسَرُّوا" (*asarrū*, "they concealed"), indicating that they are described as committing gross wrongdoing in what they concealed. Or it is a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is "أسَرُّوا النَّجْوى", placed before it for emphasis. The meaning is: they concealed the private conversation. The relative pronoun is used in place of the pronoun to record their act as wrongdoing. Or it is in the accusative of censure (*manṣūb ʿalā al-dhamm*).

His saying, ﴿Is this anything but a human being like yourselves...﴾ and so on: it is in the position of the accusative, as the object of an implied verb of saying (*qawl muḍmar*), which is an answer to a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What did they say in their private conversation?" and it was answered: "They said: Is this...", and so on. Or it is an apposition for "أسَرُّوا" or a conjunct of it, or an apposition for "النَّجْوى", meaning: they concealed this speech. "هَلْ" (*hal*) here has the sense of negation. The interrogative particle *hamza* in His saying, ﴿Will you then approach magic﴾, is for denunciation, and the *fāʾ* (*fa*, "then") is for coordination with an implied element required by the context.

His saying, ﴿while you see﴾: it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the subject of "تَأْتُونَ" (*tatūna*, "you approach"), confirming the denunciation and emphasising the improbability. The meaning is: this is nothing but a human being like yourselves, that is, of your kind, and what he brings is magic. Do you know that, so that you approach it and bring it, accepting and acquiescing, while you are witnessing that it is magic? They said this on the basis of what was fixed in their deviant belief, that the Messenger must be only an angel, and that every extraordinary thing appearing at the hand of a human being is of the category of magic. They overlooked that the sending of a human being to all humanity is what the legislative wisdom requires. May God fight them; how are they deluded! They concealed this only because it was in the manner of ratifying a covenant, arranging the beginnings of evil and corruption, and preparing the preliminaries of deception and scheming to demolish the matter of prophethood and extinguish the light of religion. But God perfects His light, even if the disbelievers dislike it. (p-55)

﴿He said: "My Lord knows the utterance in the heavens and the earth."﴾ This is a report from Him, exalted is He, of what he (peace be upon him) said after He had revealed to him their states and their words, as a clarification of the manifestness of their affair and the exposure of their secret. The choice of the expression "utterance," which encompasses both the secret and the open, rather than "secret," serves to establish His knowledge of the secret by way of demonstrative proof (al-nahj al-burhani), together with the indication that His knowledge of the secret and of the open is of one uniform degree, with no difference between them in clarity or obscurity, with certainty, as is the case with the knowledge of created beings. It is also read: "Say, 'My Lord...'" and so on. His words, exalted is He, ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ are connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial phrase (hal) describing "the utterance," meaning: existing in the heavens and the earth.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ mean: the one who is intensely knowing (al-mubalagha fi al-'ilm) of the things heard and the things known, among which are the things they kept secret in their private consultation, and so He will recompense them for their words and deeds. This is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tirad tadhyili) that confirms the content of what precedes it and contains a warning (wa'id).

**﴿Rather, they say: "Confused dreams."﴾** This is a retraction (*idrab*, a shift from one statement to another) from God, the Exalted, and a move from reporting their earlier words to reporting another, inconsistent statement that wanders through paths of falsehood. That is, they did not confine themselves to saying about him, peace be upon him, "Is this anything but a human being?" and, about what appeared at his hands of the noble Qur'an, "It is sorcery." Rather, they said: "Jumbled dreams." Then they retracted this and said: **﴿Rather, he has invented it﴾**, from his own mind, without its having any origin or semblance of an origin. Then they said: **﴿Rather, he is a poet﴾**, and what he brought is poetry that conjures for the listener meanings that have no reality. Such is the condition of the falsifier who has been refuted: he is bewildered, always vacillating between falsehood and something more false, and oscillating between corruption and something more corrupt. So the first retraction, as you see, is from God, the Exalted, while the second and third are from them. It has also been said that all of them come from them, since they retracted from their saying that it is sorcery to saying that it is jumbled dreams, then to saying that it is invented speech, and then to saying that it is the word of a poet. There is no doubt that at that point it should have been said: "They said, 'Rather, confused dreams.'" The justification that "*bal qalu*" ("Rather, they said") is a predicate of *qalu* (they said), with the implied *qalu* before the divine saying "Is this anything but a human being...", is a way of saying: "And they conspired in secret, saying: 'Is this...'" down to "Rather, confused dreams." The verb *qalu* was explicitly repeated after *bal* only because of the distance from the earlier mention, and because the sanctity of the Revelation must be protected from the likes of this.

**﴿Then let him bring us a sign﴾**: this is the answer to an omitted conditional clause, which the context makes clear. It is as if it were said: "And if he is not as we have said, but is rather a messenger from God, the Exalted, then let him bring us a sign **﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾**." That is, like the sign with which the earlier ones were sent, such as the hand and the staff and their like, so that we may believe in him. Here **"mā"** (what) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), and the place of the particle **"al-kāf"** (like) is in the genitive, as it is an attribute of *āyah* (sign). It is also permissible for *mā* to be a verbal particle (*maṣdariyyah*), in which case *al-kāf* is in the accusative, as a comparative verbal noun (*maṣdar tashbīhī*), i.e., an attribute of an omitted verbal noun. The sense is: "Then let him bring us a sign, a bringing of the kind of the sending of the earlier ones with it." The correctness of the comparison lies in the fact that bringing a sign is among the branches of sending it, i.e., a bringing that follows upon the sending. It is also permissible to understand the noble wording as meaning that both *bringing* and *sending* are intended on each side of the comparison, but mention of *sending* was omitted on the side of what is compared and mention of *bringing* on the side of what it is compared to, each being sufficient for what is omitted in the other place, as was explained at the end of Surat Yunus, peace be upon him.

﴿No town before them believed﴾ is a resumptive sentence (kalam mustaʼnaf), brought to refute them regarding what the conclusion of their speech implies, namely the implicit promise of faith, as has been pointed out. It also clarifies that in proposing those signs they are like one who seeks his own death with his own hoof, and that refusing to answer them is a way of sparing them. How could it be otherwise? Had they been given what they proposed while their unbelief was certain, their annihilation would have been necessary, due to the operation of Allah's sunnah (customary way, divine practice) concerning the earlier nations. Moreover, those who propose signs, if they are given what they proposed and then do not believe, the punishment of annihilation (istiʼsal) will certainly descend upon them without fail. The word of truth has already preceded from Him, exalted is He, that this Ummah will not be punished with the punishment of annihilation. So His saying ﴿from a town﴾ means: from the people of a town, in a place of rafʻ (nominative case) as the agent (fa'iliyyah). The "min" is superfluous (mazidah), for emphasizing generality.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We destroyed it﴾ means: by destroying its people, because they did not believe after the coming of the signs they had proposed. It is an adjectival clause (sifah) modifying "town" (qaryah).

The hamzah in His saying ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ is interrogative for denying occurrence, and the fa' is for coordination (ʻatf), either upon an implied element (muqaddar) which the hamzah entered, so that it conveys the denial of the occurrence of their belief and its negation immediately following the non-belief of the former ones. The meaning then is: no nation among the destroyed nations believed when the signs they had proposed were given; will these believe? Even if they were answered in what they asked and given what they proposed, while being more obstinate and more rebellious than those. Or, it is upon what precedes (﴿they did not believe﴾, i.e., the earlier clause), with the fa' placed before the hamzah in meaning, conveying the sequencing of the denial of their belief upon the non-belief of the former ones. The hamzah was placed before the fa' because it requires initial position (sadr), as is the view of the majority (jumhur) of grammarians.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We did not send before you any but men﴾ is a response to their saying: ﴿Is this not but a human like you?..﴾ etc. It includes a refutation of what they slipped in beneath their saying: ﴿as the former messengers were sent﴾, namely the insinuation that he, peace be upon him, is not like those messengers, may the blessings of Allah the Exalted be upon them all. For this reason, the response to their saying ﴿Then let him bring us a sign﴾ was placed before it. Also, since they said that by way of challenge (ta'jiz), it is necessary to hasten to refute and nullify it, as has passed in the explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Allah will bring it to you if He wills, and you cannot escape [Him]﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be given respite﴾. Also, because this response contains a certain expansiveness, whose placement would disturb the harmony of the parts of the noble composition. The truth is that what they took as a cause for denial is in reality a reason for affirmation, because the requirement of wisdom is that humans be sent to humans and angels to angels, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Say: Had there been in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾. For the general mass of humanity is far from being fit for angelic communication, since it depends on correspondence between the one who bestows and the one who receives. Therefore, sending an angel to them conflicts with the wisdom upon which the orbit of creation and legislation revolves. What wisdom actually requires is that an angel be sent from among them to the elite, who are distinguished by pure souls, supported by holy power, and connected to both the spiritual and the corporeal worlds, so that they may receive from one side and convey to the other.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To whom We reveal﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the manner of sending. The present tense form is for narrating a past, continuous state. The object is omitted because there is no intention to specify it. The meaning is: We did not send to the nations before your sending to your community any but men, specifically chosen from among the individuals of the species, qualified for selection and sending, to whom We reveal, through the mediation of an angel, what We reveal of laws, rulings and other things, such as narratives and reports, just as We reveal to you, without any difference between them in the reality of revelation and the reality of its meaning, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets...﴾ up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾. Just as there is no difference between you and them in humanity, why then do they not understand that you are not a novelty among the messengers, and that what has been revealed to you is not contrary to what was revealed to them, so that they would say what they say? It is also read as "yuha ilayhim" with the ya', in the passive voice, following the custom of majesty and as an announcement that the agent is determined.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr, i.e., people of earlier scripture) if you do not know﴾ is a shift of address and a turning of it toward the disbelievers, to rebuke them and bring them down from the rank of disdain and denial, following the establishment of the truth in the manner of address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he is the one worthy of address concerning such exquisite realities. As for ascertaining them by inquiry from others, that is among the duties of the common people. The fa' (then) indicates the consequence of what follows upon what precedes. The response of the condition is omitted, relying confidently on what is mentioned as an indication of it. That is: if you do not know what has been mentioned, then ask, O ignorant ones, the people of the Book (ahl al-kitab, i.e., Jews and Christians), who are acquainted with the circumstances of the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, so that your doubt may be removed. They were commanded to do so because the report of a great multitude produces knowledge, especially since they used to side with the polytheists in their enmity toward him, peace be upon him, and consult them about his affair, peace be upon him. Therefore, in this there is of the indication of the complete clarity of the matter and the strength of the standing of the Prophet (ﷺ) that is not hidden.

This clause clarifies that the messengers, peace be upon them, are an example for all members of the human species in the rules of human nature, following the statement that they are an example for them in humanity itself. *Jasad* (body) means the physical form of humans, jinn, and angels. It is in the accusative either as a second object of *ja'ala* (to make), but not in the sense of making it a body after it was not one, as is commonly meant by *tasyir* (rendering something into a state). Rather, it means making it so from the beginning, in the manner of the saying, "Glory be to the One who made the gnat small and the elephant large," as occurred in His saying, ﴿And We made the sign of the day to be seeing﴾. It may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the pronoun. The verb *ja'ala* here is *ibda'i* (originating, bringing into being from nothing). The singular *jasad* is used to indicate the genus, which also includes many individuals. It is said that there is an implied *mudaf* (a governed noun), meaning "possessors of a body."

His saying, ﴿that do not eat food﴾, is a description of it, meaning: We did not make them bodies that are free from need of eating and drinking, but rather bodies in need of that, to obtain a replacement for what dissolves from them.

﴿Nor were they immortal﴾, because the outcome of dissolution is inevitably annihilation. The choice of *ma kanu* ("they were not") over *ma ja'alnahum* ("We did not make them") is a warning that the non-eternity is required by their natural constitution, which is indicated by His saying, ﴿"Nor did We make them..."﴾, and so on, not by the newly stated making. By "immortality" is meant either a long duration, as is the case with the angels, or everlastingness, and they (the disbelievers) believed that they would not die. The meaning is: We made them bodies that are nourished, heading toward death in the end according to their appointed terms, not angels, nor bodies free from need of nourishment and protected from dissolution like the angels. Therefore they did not have immortality like theirs. Thus the sentence confirms what precedes it, that the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, were humans and not angels, along with the refutation of their saying, ﴿"What kind of messenger is this, who eats food?"﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 9:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) with what is understood from the narration of His revelation to them, Exalted is He, as a continuous, renewing revelation (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi). It is as if it were said: "We revealed to them what We revealed, then We fulfilled to them the promise which We had made to them within the revelations, namely the destruction of their enemies."

﴿So We saved them and whom We willed﴾ from the believers and others whom wisdom requires to be spared, such as one who will believe, himself or some of his descendants, in the Hereafter. This is the secret behind the protection of the Arabs from the punishment of total annihilation (al-isti'sal).

﴿And We destroyed the extravagant﴾, that is, those who exceeded the bounds (al-mujawizin lil-hudud) in disbelief and sins.

(p-58) ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf), brought to establish the truth of the Noble Qur'an, which was mentioned at the beginning of the honoured surah: the people's turning away from the signs that come to them, their mockery of it, and their calling it at one time sorcery, at another time "confused dreams," and at yet another time "fabrication" and "poetry." It also serves to explain the elevated rank of the Qur'an following the establishment of the Messenger's (ﷺ) prophethood, by showing that he is like the other noble messengers, upon whom be blessings and peace. The statement has been introduced with an oath of emphasis, to show greater concern for its content and to signal that the addressees are at the furthest degree of denial. That is: By Allah, We have indeed sent down to you, O assembly of Quraysh, ﴿a Book﴾ of great importance and of clear proof.

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿in it is your reminder﴾, it is an attribute of "a Book," confirming what the indefinite form (al-tankir al-tafkhimi, the indefiniteness that expresses magnificence) conveys of its being of lofty stature, namely that it is of beautiful effects and brings you sublime benefits. That is: in it is your honour and your fame. Compare His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. It has been said: it contains what you need in matters of your religion and your worldly affairs. It has been said: it contains what you seek of good repute through noble character. It has been said: in it is your admonition, and this is the most fitting to the context and flow of the noble arrangement, for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ is a reproachful denunciation, in which there is an urging upon them to reflect on the matter of the Book and to contemplate what lies within it of various kinds of admonitions and warnings, among which are the calamities mentioned before and after. The particle "fa" (then) is for conjunction upon an implied premise to which the statement extends, that is: Do you not reflect, so that you do not understand that the matter is so? Or: you do not understand any of the things, of which the above is one.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 11:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a town did We shatter﴾ is a kind of detailed explanation of the general statement of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾, and a clarification of the manner of their destruction and its cause, and an alert to their great number. "Kam" (how many) is khabariyyah (declarative), indicating multiplicity; its place is in the accusative, as it is the object of "qasamna" (We shattered), and "min qaryatin" (of a town) is a tamyiz (specification). In the word qasm (shattering), which is an expression for breaking by separating the parts of the broken thing and removing their composition entirely, there is an indication of the intensity of anger and the severity of wrath that is not hidden.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they were wrongdoers﴾ is in a position of genitive, as it is an attribute (sifah) of "qaryah" (town), with an omitted noun (mudaf) implied by the pronoun that follows, meaning: "And many a people of a town We shattered, who were wrongdoers in respect of the signs of Allah, exalted is He, disbelieving in them, like your own practice."

﴿And We brought into being after them﴾, that is, after their destruction, ﴿another people﴾, that is, those who were not of them by lineage nor by religion. In this there is an alert to the uprooting of the former ones and the complete cutting off of their remnant.

This is the reason for placing the narration of the creation of these (people) before the narration of the beginnings of the destruction of those, with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When they perceived Our might﴾, that is: they became fully aware of Our severe punishment, with a complete awareness, as if it were the awareness of one who witnesses something perceived by the senses.

﴿Behold, they were fleeing from it, galloping away﴾: they were running away in haste, spurring their mounts, or likened to those who do so in their extreme haste.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 13:

﴿Do not flee in haste﴾. That is: it was said to them, by the tongue of the situation or by the tongue of speech, from the angel or from whoever was there among the believers, by way of mockery and rebuke: ﴿Do not flee in haste﴾, ﴿and return to that in which you were made to live in luxury﴾. Luxury (itraf) means the indulgence in favours (ni'mah), the enjoyment and delight of comfort.

﴿And your dwellings﴾ in which you used to take pride, ﴿so that you may be questioned﴾: you are sought out for consultation (su'al), counsel (tashawur) and deliberation (tadbir) in important matters (muhimmat) and calamities (nawazil). Or: you will be missed when your dwellings are seen empty, and it will be asked, "Where are their owners?" Or: those who come to you will ask you for your gifts (nawal), on the basis that you were generous, spending your wealth ostentatiously (riya'), and miserly. So this was said to them as mockery upon mockery (tahakkum ila tahakkum).

"They said, when they despaired of escaping by fleeing and became certain of the descent of the punishment: ﴿Woe to us!﴾ That is: our destruction. ﴿Indeed we were wrongdoers﴾ That is: deserving of the punishment. This is their acknowledgment of wrongdoing and of its consequence, the punishment, and their regret over it at a time when it no longer benefited them."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 15:

﴿So that was their claim⁠—﴾ That is: they kept repeating that same phrase. Calling it "da'wa" (claim, or call) means "da'wa" in the sense of a summons, because the one who utters it is, as it were, calling out to destruction, saying: "O woe, come! This is your time."

﴿until We made them a harvest⁠—﴾ That is: like a harvest, and "hasid" means what is reaped from crops and plants; for this reason it is not made plural.

﴿extinguished.﴾ That is: dead, from "khamadat al-nar" (the fire went out) when it is extinguished. It and "hasidan" together occupy the position of the second object of "ja'ala" (to make), as in your saying: "I made it sweet, sour." The meaning is: We made them gathered together in their likeness to a harvest and to extinguished embers. Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the object "ja'alnahum," or from the concealed pronoun in "hasidan," or an attribute of "hasidan," which we count as a meaning, since it is in the sense of "ja'alnahum amthal hasid" (We made them like a harvest).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 21, verse 16:**

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth﴾ is a general indication that the creation of the world and the origination of the children of Adam are founded upon the principles of profound wisdoms, which entail lofty ends. It also alerts that the terrible punishment and the descending retribution that have been related concerning the people of the cities are among the requirements of those wisdoms and their ramifications, according to what their deeds necessitated. It also alerts that those addressed who follow in their footsteps have sins like theirs. That is, We did not create them ﴿and what is between them﴾ of creatures whose kinds and individuals cannot be counted, and whose types and units cannot be restricted, in this wondrous pattern and impregnable method, empty of wisdoms and benefits. He expressed this by play and sport, saying ﴿playing﴾, to show the perfection of His exaltation above creation devoid of wisdom, by depicting it in a form about whose impossibility of issuing from Him, glorified is He, no one doubts. Rather, We created them and what is between them only so that they would be a beginning for the existence of man, a cause for his livelihood, and a sign guiding him to attaining Our knowledge, which is the highest goal, through obedience to Us and worship of Us. This is what His saying, exalted is He, expresses: ﴿And He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 17:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾, it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it regarding the negation of play and diversion. That is: had We wished to take something with which one amuses oneself and plays, ﴿We would have taken it from Us﴾, that is, from the side of Our power, or "from Our presence," of what befits Our dignity, from the pure immaterial beings (al-mujarradat), not from raised bodies and placed masses, like the custom of tyrants in raising thrones and beautifying them, and levelling carpets and adorning them. But Our wishing it is impossible, since wisdom escapes it, so Our taking it is impossible with certainty.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿if We were doers﴾, the object of the verb is omitted, relying on what precedes it as evidence for it. That is: if We were doers, We would have taken it. It has been said that "in" (in) is a negation particle, meaning: We were not doers, that is, of taking diversion, because We do not will it. In that case it is an explanation for the negation of the consequent due to the negation of the antecedent. Or [it is an explanation] for the will to take it, in which case it is an explanation for the negation of the antecedent, which necessitates the negation of the consequent. It has been said: al-lahw (diversion) means "child" in the dialect of Yemen, and it has been said: "wife." The intended meaning is a refutation of the Christians, but its remoteness is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 18:

﴿Nay, We hurl the truth upon falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes.﴾ This is a turning away from the adoption of play (lahw), or rather from the desire for it, as if it were said: "We would not desire it; rather, it is Our way to overcome the truth, of which seriousness (jidd) is a part, over falsehood, of which play is a kind. The specific mention of this matter from among all His other matters, may He be exalted, serves as a transition to the threat that follows."

﴿fa-yadmaghuhu﴾ means: He utterly annihilates it, just as We did to the people of the cities that are recounted. The verb "qadhf" (hurling), which is the forceful casting of a solid body such as a rock, has been borrowed to express the bringing of the truth upon falsehood. And for His annihilation of falsehood, "dam'" (crushing) has been borrowed, which is the breaking of a soft, hollow thing, namely the brain, in such a way that it splits its membrane, leading to the departure of the soul, as a depiction of it by that. It was read as "fa-yadmaghuhu" in the accusative, but this is weak. It was also read as "fa-yadmaghuhu" with a damma on the mim.

﴿fa-idha huwa zahiqun﴾ means: he is utterly gone. In the sudden "idha" and the nominal sentence there is an indication of the perfection of hastening in departing and perishing, which is not hidden; it is as if it were perishing from its very root.

﴿Woe to you for what you describe﴾ is a threat to the Quraysh that for them too there is a like punishment and retribution to that of those (peoples). The "min" is causal (ta'lilliyyah), related to the stability (istiqrar) to which the predicate is attached, or to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "al-wayl" or of its pronoun in the predicate. The "ma" is either verbal-masdariyyah, or relative (mawsulah), or descriptive (mawsufah), meaning: woe and destruction have become established for you because of your describing Him, glory be to Him, with what does not befit His majestic station, or with that which you ascribe to Him of offspring, or being whatever you describe Him, exalted be He, with.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 19:

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that confirms what precedes it: that He, exalted is He, created all His creatures upon profound wisdom and perfect order, and that He establishes the truth and nullifies falsehood. That is, to Him alone, exalted is He, belong all creatures, in creation, dominion, governance, disposal, giving life, causing death, punishment and reward, without anyone having any share in that, whether independently or as a subordinate.

﴿And those with Him﴾ are the angels, peace be upon them. He referred to them by this phrase right after referring to them as "whoever is in the heavens," to elevate them in honor before Him, mighty and exalted, and their nearness to Him is like the standing of those brought near to kings, by way of analogy. It is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿they do not disdain to worship Him﴾, that is, they do not exalt themselves above it, nor do they regard themselves as great.

﴿And they do not tire﴾, that is, they do not grow weary, they do not become exhausted, and they do not grow faint. The form of istif'al, which indicates intensification of exhaustion (husur), is used to draw attention to the fact that their acts of worship, by their weight and continuity, are truly deserving of causing exhaustion, and yet they do not become exhausted. The particle "la" serves to negate intensified exhaustion while the root of exhaustion is affirmed in general. Likewise, the negation of being a tyrant (zalamiyya) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I am not one who wrongs the servants﴾ serves to indicate the abundance of injustice that might be supposed to be directed at the servants, not to negate intensified injustice while the root of injustice is affirmed in general. It has been said: "those with Him" is conjoined to the first "whoever," and singling them out by mention despite their being included in "whoever is in the heavens and the earth" is for magnification, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾. In that case, His saying, exalted is He, "they do not disdain," is then a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the second group.

They glorify Him night and day: that is, they declare Him far above all imperfection, magnify Him, and extol Him continually at all times. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that comes in answer to a question arising from what precedes it, as though it were said: "What do they do in their acts of worship?" or "How do they worship?" So it is said: "They glorify..." etc. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "yastahsirun" (they grow weary).

Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They do not slacken﴾, that is, their glorification is never interrupted by any pause at all, whether through leisure or through some other occupation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 21:

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who can raise the dead?﴾ This is a narration of another of their offences, by way of a transition (inḍrāb) and a shift (intiqāl) from one kind of reproach to another, following the establishment of the truth by demonstrating that He, exalted is He, created all creatures according to the course of wisdom, that they are all under His dominion (malakūt) and subjugation (qahr), that His servants submit to His obedience and persist in His worship, glorifying Him above everything that is not fitting to His majesty, among which are rivals (andād). The meaning of the interrogative hamza in the disjunctive "am" (am munqaṭi'a) is the denial of what is occurring. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from the earth﴾ is connected to "they have taken" (ittakhadhū), or to an omitted element that is an attribute of "gods" (ālihah). In either case, the intent is belittlement (taḥqīr), not specification (takhṣīs).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they raise up﴾, that is, they resurrect the dead, is an attribute of "gods" (ālihah). What the denial, the ignorance-attribution, and the censure revolve around is the very act of taking them, for it is certainly occurring; that is: rather, they have taken gods from the earth, themselves specifically, despite their lowliness and inanimateness, who raise the dead. Not at all, for what they have taken as gods is far removed from that. Although they did not state this explicitly, yet inasmuch as they claimed divinity for them, it is as though they claimed for them the raising of the dead, since it is necessarily one of the divine attributes definitively. The meaning of specification in the fronting of the pronoun is what has been pointed out: alerting to the complete incongruity of their state with raising the dead, which necessitates greater denial, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾ and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Was it at God and His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾, for the fronting of the prepositional phrase serves to alert to the complete incongruity of His command with being doubted or mocked. It is also permissible to make this one of the consequences of their false claim, because divinity necessitates independent authority in originating and restoring; so inasmuch as they claimed divinity for the idols, it is as though they claimed for them independent authority in raising the dead, just as they were thereby made claimants to the very principle of raising the dead.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 22:

﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah﴾ is a refutation of the plurality of gods, by establishing the proof not merely for its non-existence but for its impossibility. The mention of the plural form (ālihah) is due to its occurrence right after the denial of taking gods (ittikhādh al-ālihah), and not because plurality has any role in the argument. Likewise is the supposition of their being in them (fīhimā). And "illā" is in the sense of "ghayr" (other than), being an attribute of "gods" (ālihah), and there is no room for it to be an exception (istithnā'), because the inclusion of what precedes it in what follows it is impossible, and this would lead to corruption of the meaning, since it would then indicate that the corruption is due to their being in them without Him, the Exalted. Nor is it in the nominative case as a substitute (badal), because that is a branch of the exception and is conditional upon being in a non-affirmative statement. That is: Had there been in the heavens and the earth gods other than Allah, as they falsely believe, ﴿they would have been corrupted﴾, i.e., both would have been ruined along with what is in them. Since the consequent is negated, the negation of the antecedent is known with certainty. The explanation of the implication (mulāzamah) is that divinity necessarily entails the power to exercise sole control over them absolutely, by alteration, change, origination, annihilation, giving life and causing death. So their remaining as they are is either due to the influence of each of them, which is impossible, because it is impossible for a specific effect to occur from multiple causes; or due to the influence of one of them, in which case the rest are certainly excluded from divinity. Know that making the consequent their corruption after their existence is because the plurality of gods in them was taken into account in the antecedent; otherwise, the proof requires the impossibility of plurality absolutely, for if the god were plural, then if all agreed upon the desired outcome, the powers would be in mutual competition over it, and if they disagreed, (p-62) they would obstruct one another, and then nothing would exist at all; and since the consequent is negated, the negation of the antecedent is determined. The particle "fa" in His, the Exalted, saying ﴿So glory be to Allah﴾ is for the consequence of what follows it from what precedes it, namely the established oneness by proof. That is: so glorify Him with the glorification proper to Him, and exalt Him above what is not befitting to Him, among the matters of which one is that He should have a partner in divinity. The mention of the divine name in place of the pronoun is to indicate the reason for the ruling, for divinity is the basis of all His attributes of perfection, among which is His transcendence above what is not befitting to Him, and to instill awe and bring about reverence.

And His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾ is an attribute of the noble name, emphasizing His transcendence, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿Above what they describe﴾ is connected to the glorification, that is: so glorify Him above what they ascribe to Him, namely that there should be gods besides Him.

"He cannot be questioned about what He does" — a resumption (isti'naf) explaining that, because of the immensity of His greatness and the might of His overpowering dominion, none of His creatures may dispute with Him or ask Him about His actions, following the statement that He has no partner in divinity. "But they will be questioned" — that is, the servants will be questioned about what they do, down to the smallest detail (naqir and qitmir), because they are owned by Him, exalted be He, and are made to serve Him. In this there is a warning (wa'id) to the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 24:

﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ This is a shift (idrab, a turning from one matter to another) and a transition from demonstrating the falsehood of their claim that what they have taken are gods in truth, by showing that they are devoid of the attributes of divinity, among which is resurrection (inshar), and by establishing a decisive proof of the impossibility of there being a plurality of gods in any sense, and of His glory's exclusive possession of divinity, to demonstrating the falsehood of their taking those gods, which are utterly bereft of those attributes, as partners to God, mighty is His authority; and rebuking them by compelling them to establish proof for their false claim, and confirming that all the heavenly books speak to the truth of monotheism (tawhid) and the falsehood of associating partners (shirk). The hamza (alif of interrogation, hamza) serves to deny the said taking and to declare it abhorrent and grave. "Min" (from) is connected to "ittakhadhu" (they have taken), and the meaning is: rather, they have taken, going beyond Him, exalted is He, despite the manifestation of His glorious affairs which necessitate His exclusive divinity, gods, despite the manifest absence of the special qualities of divinity from them altogether.

﴿Say﴾ to them, by way of rebuke and silencing: ﴿Bring your proof﴾ for what you claim, whether from the standpoint of reason (aql) or transmission (naql), for there is no validity to a statement that has no evidence for it in religious matters, especially in such a grave affair. And the attribution of "proof" (burhan) to their pronoun carries the implication that they have a proof, which is a form of mockery of them.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾ are an illumination of His proof and an indication that it is among what all the divine books have spoken of and what the tongues of all the earlier messengers have testified to, and an increase in stirring them to establish proof, to reveal the completeness of their incapacity. That is: this revelation concerning monotheism, which includes the decisive rational proof, is the reminder of my community, that is, their admonition, and the reminder of the earlier nations, which I have established, so you too establish your proof. It has been said: the meaning is: this is the book revealed to my community, and this is the book revealed to the communities of the prophets, peace be upon them, from the three books and the scrolls; so consult them and see whether in any one of them there is anything other than the command to monotheism and the prohibition of associating partners. Therein is a rebuke to them, containing the affirmation of the opposite of their claim. It has also been read with tanwin and with the active construction, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan﴾, and with it and with "min" as a preposition, on the basis that "ma'a" is a noun that is a time-adverb, like "qabl" and "ba'd".

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, most of them do not know the truth﴾ (p-63) are a shift on His part, not part of the dictated speech, and a transition from the command to rebuke them by demanding proof to an explanation that the argument does not succeed with them by manifesting the truth of the truth and the falsehood of falsehood, for most of them do not comprehend the truth nor distinguish between it and falsehood.

﴿So they are﴾ for that reason ﴿turning away﴾, that is, continuing persistently in turning away from monotheism and from following the Messenger, not refraining from their error and misguidance, even though clear signs and proofs are repeated upon them; or turning away from what has been cast upon them of rational and transmitted proofs. It has been read: "al-haqq" (the truth) in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, standing between the cause and the effect, as an emphasis of causality.

The words of His Exalted saying: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾ are a resumed statement (isti'naf) that confirms what was left general (ujmila) in the preceding verses, namely that monotheism (al-tawhid) is something the divine scriptures (al-kutub al-ilahiyya) have declared and upon which the messengers, peace be upon them, have all agreed.

It has been read as "yuhha" (yūḥā), in the third-person form with the passive voice (mabniyyan li-l-maf'ul). In either case, the present-tense form (sighat al-mudari') is used to recount a past situation (hikayat al-hal al-madiya), so as to bring the image of the revelation vividly before the mind (istihdaran li-surat al-wahy).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 26:

﴿And they say: "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ This is a narration of the offence of a group of the polytheists, brought in to demonstrate its falsehood and to state the exaltation of Allah, the Exalted, above it, immediately after the statement of His glorification above partners in every respect. They were a tribe of Khuza'ah, who say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah, the Exalted." Al-Wahidi (al-Wahidi, the Qur'an commentator) transmitted that Quraysh and some kinds of the Arabs, namely Juhayna, Banu Salama, Khuza'ah, and Banu Malih, used to say this. The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman), which indicates that everything other than Him, the Exalted, is nurtured by Him or is a recipient of His blessing, is made to bring out the full monstrosity of their false statement.

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: that is, He is exalted in His essence with the exaltation befitting Him. The word subhan (glorification, exaltation) may be a verbal noun from sabaha, meaning "he removed far," or "I glorify Him with His glorification," taking it as a proper noun for glorification, which is spoken by the tongues of the servants; or it may mean "glorify Him with His glorification."

As for His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Rather, they are servants﴾: this is a turning away from and a nullification of what they said, as if it were said: "The angels are not as they claim; rather, they are servants of Him, the Exalted." ﴿Honoured﴾: brought near to Him. It has been read as "mukarramun" with the doubled letter (ra), and in this there is an indication of the source of the people's error.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 21, verse 27:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, is another attribute of the servants, indicating the completeness of their obedience and submission to His command, Exalted is He. That is, they do not say anything until He says it or commands them to say it. Its underlying sense is: "Their speech does not precede His speech, Exalted is He." So the act of preceding is attributed to them and linked to Him, treating the preceding of their speech over His speech as if it were their preceding Him, Exalted is He. This is for greater exaltation of them above that, and to draw attention to the extreme repugnance of preceding, which is aimed at those who say what God Most High has not said. He made speech the place of preceding and its instrument. Then the preposition *lam* (لِ) was substituted for the possessive construction, for brevity and to avoid repetition.

It is also read as *لا يَسْبِقُونَهُ* (*la yasbiqunahu*) with a *ḍamma* on the *bā'* (*yasbiqūnahu*), from *sābaqtuhu, fasabaqtuhu, asbiquhu*. In this reading there is further repugnance toward preceding, and an indication that whoever's speech precedes the speech of God Most High has set himself up to contend with Him in precedence, and so has outstripped Him and overcome Him, and we seek refuge in God Most High. It also adds further exaltation of them, by clarifying that such preceding is, in their view, like being overcome after contending. Thus the statement comes to suggest that such a thing could be issued by them, which is what is denied of them.

﴿And they act by His command﴾ is a statement of their following Him in deeds, after the statement of their following Him in words. The denial that they precede Him in speech is an expression of their following Him in speech. It is as if it were said: they speak by His command and act by His command, not by any other command at all. The restriction (*qaṣr*) derived from fronting the prepositional phrase is to be understood in relation to what is other than His command, not in relation to the command of others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 28:

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ This is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) which comes as a justification (taʿlil) for what precedes it and as a preparation (tamhid) for what follows it. For their knowledge of His (exalted is He) encompassing of what they have put forward and put off, of words and deeds, means that they are ever watchful over their own states, so they are not able to say any word or do any deed without His command (exalted is He).

﴿And they do not intercede except for whom He is pleased with﴾ that He should intercede for him, out of awe of Him (exalted is He). ﴿And they﴾ along with that ﴿from fear of Him﴾ (Mighty and Majestic is He) ﴿are apprehensive﴾, that is, trembling. The root of khashyah (fear accompanied by reverence) is fear together with glorification, and for this reason it is specific to the scholars ('ulama'). Ishfaq (apprehension) is fear together with care (iʿtina'). So when it is transitive with min, the sense of fear in it is more apparent, and when it is transitive with ʿala, the matter is reversed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 29:

﴿And whoever among them says﴾ That is, among the angels, — the discussion concerns them and their being far removed from what they have been attributed with — ﴿"Indeed, I am a god besides Him"﴾ transgressing Him, exalted is He, ﴿then that one﴾ — the one whose saying has been supposed as a supposition of impossibility — ﴿We shall recompense with Hell﴾ like all other criminals. And the mention of their praiseworthy qualities and their pleasing deeds will not avail them. In this there is an indication of the strength of His dominion, exalted is He, the might of His majesty, and the impossibility that the angels could be in a state where what those disbelievers imagined about them could be imagined, which is not hidden.

﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ — the phrase is an infinitive of comparison (maṣdar tashbīhī) emphasizing the content of what precedes it. That is: "Like that dreadful recompense, We recompense those who place things in other than their proper places and transgress their bounds." The restriction (qaṣr) derived from the fronting (taqdīm) is considered in relation to deficiency, not excess; that is, there is no recompense less than it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 30:

﴿Have not those who disbelieve seen?﴾ This is a rebuke directed at them for their failure to reflect upon the cosmic signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah) which indicate that God, exalted is He, alone deserves divinity, and that all else besides Him is subjugated under His dominion (malakut). The hamzah is for censure (al-inkar), and the waw is for coordination (al-'atf) with an implied (muqaddar) clause. It is also recited without the waw, and the seeing is cognitive (qalbiyyah), meaning: "Have they not reflected and known" ﴿that the heavens and the earth were﴾, i.e., the heavens and the earths were joined together, as in God's saying: ﴿Indeed, God holds back the heavens and the earth lest they should cease﴾.

﴿joined⁠ (ratqan)⁠﴾ Al-ratq means to close up and to be fused together. The meaning is either by omitting a noun (al-mudaf) so that it means "both were possessors of ratq," or it has the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "both were fused together." It is also recited as "ratqan shay'an ratqan," meaning "fused."

﴿Then We parted them⁠ (fatqnahuma)⁠﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, in a narration of 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they were one single thing bound together, then God, exalted is He, separated them, raised the heaven to where it is, and kept the earth in place. Ka'b said: God created the heavens and the earth adhering to each other, then He created a wind that came between them and split them apart. From al-Hasan: God created the earth at the place of Bayt al-Maqdis in the shape of a grinding stone (al-fihr), upon which was smoke clinging to it. Then He raised the smoke, created the heavens from it, held the grinding stone in its place, and spread out the earth from it. This is His saying: ﴿They were joined, then We parted them﴾. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: the heavens were one fused layer, and He split it and made it seven heavens; likewise the earth was one raised layer, and He split it and made it seven earths. Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of 'Ata', and upon it most of the exegetes agree, said: the heavens were fused, level and solid, not raining, and the earth was fused, not producing plants; so He split the heaven with rain and the earth with vegetation. Thus the intended meaning of "the heavens" is the lowest heaven, and the plural is in consideration of its horizons, or "the heavens" altogether, since they have a role in rainfall. The disbelievers knew the ratq and fatq in this meaning without any doubt. As for the earlier meanings, they, although they did not know them, were nonetheless able to know them, either through reflection and contemplation, since splitting is an accidental state requiring an eternal agent, or through inquiry from scholars and consulting books.

﴿And We made from water every living thing⁠﴾ i.e., We created from water every living animal, as in God's saying: ﴿And God created every creature from water﴾. This is because water is among its greatest materials, or because of their extreme need for it and benefit from it, or it means We made every living thing from water, i.e., by means of a cause from it which it necessarily requires. The fronting of the second object is for emphasis upon it, not merely because the two objects are originally subject and predicate, and the predicate, when it is an adverbial phrase, should precede the subject; for that is a purely permissible and preferable matter. It is also recited as "hayyan" (living), either as an adjective of "kull" or as a second object; and the adverbial phrase, as in the first case, is placed before the object for emphasis upon it and eagerness toward what is delayed.

﴿Will they not then believe?⁠﴾ This is a censure for their not believing in God alone, despite the manifestation of what necessarily requires it of the cosmic and personal signs which indicate His unique singularity, exalted and majestic is He, in divinity, and that all else among His creatures is subjugated under His dominion and power. The fa' is for coordination with an implied clause required by the preceding censure, i.e., "Do they know that and yet not believe?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 31:

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾ i.e., stable mountains, the plural of rasiyah (رَاسِيَةٍ), from rasa al-shay' (رَسا الشَّيْءُ), meaning: when a thing became fixed and firmly settled. It is an adjective that takes the masculine plural form (jam' al-mudhakkar) yet is used for the feminine plural with non-rational beings, which is not in doubt as to its soundness, like His saying, exalted is He: "ashhurun ma'lumat" (months well-known) and "ayyaman ma'dudat" (days numbered).

﴿Lest it should shake with them﴾ i.e., out of aversion to it moving and quaking with them; or "lest it should shake with them," with the lam (لام) elided, and not for the absence of ambiguity.

﴿And We placed therein﴾ i.e., in the earth. The repetition of the verb is due to the difference between the two things placed, and to fulfil the due right of the context of favour; or [it refers] to the firm mountains, because they are the ones in need of paths.

﴿Broad roads (fijaj)﴾ wide passages. It was placed before His saying, exalted is He, ﴿subulan (paths)﴾, though it is a description of it, so that it becomes a circumstantial qualifier (hal), thereby indicating that when He created them He created them thus; or so that it becomes a substitute (badal) for them, the paths, thereby implicitly indicating that He created them and widened them for travellers, along with the emphasis this carries.

﴿That they may be guided﴾ i.e., to their interests and their necessities.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 32:

﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾ protected from falling by Our overpowering might, or from decay and dissolution until the appointed time by Our will, or from eavesdropping by means of shooting stars.

﴿And they, from its signs﴾ those which indicate His oneness, His knowledge, His wisdom, His power and His will, some of which are perceptible to the senses and some of which are known through investigation in the sciences of nature (ʿilm al-ṭabīʿa) and cosmology (ʿilm al-hayʾa) ﴿are turning away﴾ they do not reflect upon them, so they remain upon the disbelief and misguidance in which they are.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 33:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾, which are their two signs, is an explanation of some of those signs from which they turn away, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), which necessitates emphasis on the import of the speech; that is, it is He who created them alone.

﴿Each﴾, i.e., each one of them, with the tanwin being a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted.

﴿in an orbit they swim﴾, i.e., they move across the surface of the orbit like swimming in water. The orbit (falak) here refers to the genus, as when you say: "The caliph clothed them in a robe." The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the sun and the moon. It is permissible for the two to be mentioned alone with it because there is no ambiguity, and the pronoun refers to them both; the plural is in consideration of their risings. The pronoun was made the plural masculine of rational beings (waw al-'uqala') because swimming is their state.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 34:

﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity﴾, that is, in this world, because it would contradict the cosmic wisdom (al-hikmah al-takwiniyyah) and the legislative wisdom (al-hikmah al-tashri'iyyah). ﴿So if you die﴾, in accordance with Our wisdom, ﴿will they be the immortals?﴾ It was revealed when they said: ﴿We await for him the vicissitudes of time﴾. The fa' (fa) here links the conditional clause to what precedes it, and the hamzah (hamzah) is for denying its content after the establishment of the universal principle that negates it entirely. The denial and negation of their immortality is intended to deny what it depends on, in existence and non-existence: their gloating at his death ﷺ. For gloating at what befalls him is also something that a rational person should not do. It is as if it were said: "So if you die, will they be the immortals, so that they may gloat at your death?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 35:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾, i.e., tasting the bitterness of separating from its body, a proof of what they denied concerning your immortality.

﴿And We test you﴾. The address is either to people in general, by way of tilwin (shift in mode of address), or to the disbelievers, by way of iltifat (shift in grammatical person), i.e., We deal with you as one who tests you ﴿with evil and good﴾, with calamities and blessings, to see whether you will be patient and thankful or not.

﴿Fitnah﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing "nabluwakum" (We test you), coming from its own root but not from its exact wording (ghayr lafzih).

﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾, not to other than Us, neither independently nor in partnership. So We will recompense you according to the deeds that appear from you. On the first reading, this is both promise and threat; on the second, it is pure threat. It also hints that the purpose of this worldly life is trial and exposure to reward and punishment. It was also read as "yurja'un" (they will be returned) with the yaa', by way of iltifat.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 36:

﴿And when those who disbelieve see you, they take you not but as a mockery﴾. That is, the polytheists. ﴿"Is this the one who mentions your gods?"﴾ [They say this] on the presumption of a verb of saying; that is, they say or are saying that, meaning: he mentions them with disparagement, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"We heard a youth mentioning them..."﴾ etc.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they, at the mention of the Most Merciful, are disbelievers﴾, it is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the implied pronoun of the presumed saying. The meaning is: they find fault with him, peace be upon him, for mentioning their gods, which neither harm nor benefit, with disparagement, while they themselves, at the mention of the Most Merciful, who has bestowed favours upon them with what befits Him of monotheism, or with guiding creation through sending messengers and revealing books, or with the Qur'an, are disbelievers; so they are deserving of blame and denunciation. Thus the first pronoun is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "disbelievers" (kāfirūn), and "at the mention of" (bi-dhikri) is a complement connected to the predicate, and the implied sense is: "and they are disbelievers at the mention of the Most Merciful." The second pronoun is a verbal emphasis (ta'kīd lafẓī) of the first, so there occurred a separation between the governing element and its governed element by the emphasized term, and between the emphasizer and the emphasized by the governed element.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 37:

﴿Man was created of haste.﴾ He is described as if he were made of haste, because of his excessive eagerness and his lack of patience. This is a way of treating the dispositions he was created with as if they were the very substances he was created from, which indicates how constantly they cling to him and how inseparable they are from him. Among his haste is his rushing toward disbelief and his urgency in seeking the threatened punishment. It is related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he hastened the punishment by saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us...﴾ to the end of the verse. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended "man" is Adam, peace be upon him, and that when the spirit reached his chest but had not fully penetrated it, he wanted to stand up. It is further related that when the spirit entered his eyes, he looked at the fruits of Paradise, and when it entered his body, he craved food. It has also been said that Allah created him at the end of the day, on Friday, before the sun set, and so He hastened to create him before it disappeared. The meaning then is: man was created as a creature originating from haste, and the mention of it explains that haste is among the motives of his hastiness in matters. The more apparent view is that the intended meaning is the species as a whole, even though the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, extends to his descendants. It has also been said that *al-ʿajal* means clay in the language of Himyar, but this has no relevance here.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will show you My signs﴾, it is a shift in address (*talwin al-khitab*, a change of addressee), turning the speech away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to those who were hastening, in the manner of threat and warning. That is, "I will show you My retributions in the Hereafter, such as the punishment of the Fire and other things."

﴿So do not seek to hasten it﴾ by bringing it about, and it is a prohibition against what their souls have been disposed toward, in order to restrain them from what they desire.

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ That is, at the time of the coming of the Hour that they were threatened with. They said it out of haste for its arrival, by way of mockery (*istihza'*) and denial, as the answer indicates, and not out of a request to specify its time by way of a binding challenge (*ilzam*), as in Surat al-Mulk.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ That is, in your promise that it will come to us. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to the believers who recite the noble verses that announce the coming of the Hour. The response to the conditional is omitted, relying on what precedes it as an indication, just as it is omitted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾. Their saying, ﴿When is this promise?﴾ is a expression of impatience on their part regarding the promised thing and a demand for its arrival by way of haste, since that is in effect a command to bring it quickly. It is as if it were said: "Then let it come to us swiftly, if you are truthful."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 39:**

﴿If only those who disbelieve knew﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new clause that begins a fresh statement) brought to explain the severity of the terror of what they are hastening for, and the horror of the punishment in it, and that they only hasten for it because of their ignorance of its reality. The use of the present tense in the conditional clause, although the meaning is past, serves to convey the continuation of their lack of knowledge. A negated present verb in the position of a past verb is not explicit in conveying the negation of the continuation of the action. Rather, it indicates the continuation of its negation as well, according to the context, as in your saying: "If you were kind to me, I would thank you," where the meaning is that the absence of thanks is due to the continuing absence of kindness, not to the discontinuation of kindness. Placing the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) in the position of the pronoun is to draw attention, through what is in the relative clause (*silah*), to the cause of their hastening.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when they will not be able to keep the Fire off their faces or their backs﴾ is the object of "knows" (*ya'lamu*). It is an expression for the promised time which they were hastening for. Its being added to the sentence that functions as a qualifier (*jumlah jariyah majra al-sifah*), whose attribution to the qualified thing should be known to the addressee as well, despite the disbelievers' denial of it, is to indicate that it is so evident that there is no need to inform of it. Rather, its proper place is among the established facts that are taken for granted. The apodosis of "if" (*law*) is omitted, meaning: If their lack of knowledge of the time they are hastening for did not continue, through their saying: ﴿When is this promise?﴾, from the moment at which the Fire surrounds them from every side.

The specification of the faces and backs by mention, in the sense of the front and the back, is because they are the most well-known sides. The fact that encompassment by them implies encompassment of the whole, such that they cannot repel it by themselves from any one of their sides.

﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ from the direction of others in repelling it, etc., because of what they did of hastening. It is permissible that "knows" (*ya'lamu*) be intransitive with its object omitted, being treated as an intransitive verb, meaning: If they had knowledge, they would not have done what they did. His saying, exalted is He: "a time…" etc. is a resumptive sentence that confirms their ignorance and explains its continuation until that time, as if it were said: When they see what they see, they will know the reality of the situation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 40:

﴿Rather, it will come upon them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿they will not hold it back﴾; that is, they will not hold it back, but rather it will come upon them, i.e., the promise (al-ʿidda), or the Fire (al-nār), or the Hour (al-sāʿa).

﴿Suddenly, and it will confound them﴾, i.e., it will overwhelm them or bewilder them. It has also been read with the verbs in the masculine form, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the promise (al-waʿd) or the time (al-ḥīn). Likewise the pronoun (hāʾ) in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so they will not be able to repel it﴾ (fa-lā yastaṭīʿūna raddahā), by interpreting the promise as the Fire, or the appointed term (al-ʿidda) and the time (al-ḥīn) as the Hour. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the Fire. It has been said that it refers to the suddenness (al-baghta), i.e., they will not be able to repel it from themselves entirely.

﴿Nor will they be given respite﴾, i.e., they will not be granted a moment's delay in which to rest, and in this is a reminder of their being granted respite in the world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 41:

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked﴾. It is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning their mockery of him (ﷺ), within the context of their urging for haste, and an implicit promise that there will befall them the like of what befell those who mocked the earlier messengers, upon them be prayer and peace. Its introduction with an oath serves to further confirm its content. The tanwin on "al-Rusul" (messengers) is for magnification and multiplication. And "min" (from) is connected to an omitted element which is a qualifier of it, meaning: "By Allah, indeed messengers of great station and of great number were mocked," or "were resolved" or something similar, for its meaning revolves around comprehensiveness and necessity, and it is hardly used except for evil and for what encompasses a person of the disliked deed he has done.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿those who mocked them﴾, meaning: of those messengers, upon them be peace, is connected to "haqa" (befell). Its placement before its subject, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿what they used to mock﴾, is for the sake of hastening to clarify that evil has reached them. And "ma" is either a relative pronoun, conveying magnification, with the pronoun in the genitive referring back to it, and the preposition-phrase connected to the verb; its placement before the verb is for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil), meaning: "So there encompassed them that which they used to mock, when they were destroyed on account of it." Or it is a verbal-masdar ("ma masdariyya"), in which case the pronoun in the genitive refers then to the category of the Messenger, indicated by the plural, as they said. Perhaps the choice of the singular over the plural is to alert that the requital of their mockery befalls them for each single one of them, peace be upon him, and not the requital of their mockery of all of them as a whole only; meaning: "So there descended upon them the requital of their mockery," placing the cause in the place of the cause, to signal the complete connection between the two. Or it is the very mockery itself, if by that is meant the otherworldly punishment, based on the embodiment of deeds, for the outward deeds in this world take on substantive forms in the next world, corresponding to them in goodness and ugliness. (p-69) Upon this the weighing is built, and its details have already passed in (Surat al-A'raf). And in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Your rebellion is only against yourselves...﴾ the verse, to its end.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 42:

﴿Say﴾: an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), following his consolation with what was mentioned of their affair coming to destruction, and a command to him, peace be upon him, to say to those mockers, by way of rebuke and reproach: ﴿Who will keep you safe﴾, i.e., will guard you, ﴿by night and by day from the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., from His punishment, which you deserve to have descend upon you by night or by day. Or the mention of the night first is because calamities occur more often in it and strike harder. In the use of the title "the Most Merciful" there is an indication that their protector is nothing but His general mercy. After he, peace be upon him, was commanded to ask in the manner mentioned, in accordance with what their state requires, because they are such that, were it not that Allah the Exalted guards them in both periods of day and night, every kind of calamity would have befallen them, they are deserving of being required to acknowledge this, and then be rebuked for the polytheism they are upon.
