He turned away from that with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, but they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, explaining that they have another state which calls for diverting the address away from them, namely that they do not bring the remembrance of Him, the Exalted, to their minds, let alone fear His punishment, or count their security and ease in which they were as guarding and protection, so that they would ask about the protector, in the manner of the saying of the one who said:

"Turn aside and greet the abode's remains for Nu'm, the ruins of the dwelling... What are you greeting of the mound and stones?"

And in the linking of turning away to the remembrance of Him, the Exalted, and the mention of the name "Lord" annexed to their pronoun, which indicates that they are under His dominion, management and nurture, the Exalted, there is an implication, which is not hidden, that they are in the furthest extreme of misguidance and error.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 43:

The word "am" (or, "rather," "or") in His saying, ﴿Or do they have gods that protect them from Us?﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and what it carries of the meaning of "bal" (rather) is for turning away (idrab) and moving on (intiqal) from what precedes it, namely the explanation that their ignorance of His protecting them is due to their lack of fear, which arises from their turning away entirely from the remembrance of their Lord, to a rebuke of them for relying on their gods and attributing protection to them. The hamzah (interrogative particle) is for denying that they have gods able to do that, and the meaning is: Do they have gods that protect them from the punishment, surpassing Our protection or Our preservation, or from a punishment coming from Us, so that they rely upon them and are confident in their preservation? In directing the denial and negation at the existence of gods described with the attribute of protection mentioned, rather than at the attribute itself by saying, "Do their gods protect them..." and so on, there is an indication of the removal of those gods from the rank of existence, let alone the rank of protection, which is not hidden.

And His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿They are not able to help themselves, nor will they be accompanied (in protection) from Us.﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it of denial and clarifying the falsity of their belief. That is: they are not able to help themselves, and they will not be accompanied with help from Our side. So how could it be supposed that they could help others?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 44:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, We gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until a long life passed over them﴾ is a turning away (idrab, a shift of direction) from what they had imagined, by clarifying that the reason for their being preserved is Our granting them enjoyment through the deeds that He decreed for them; or, [it is a turning away] from indicating its falsehood, the clarification of what caused them to imagine that is that He, the Exalted, granted them enjoyment of the life of this world and gave them respite until their lifespans lengthened, so they reckoned that they would continue thus, and that it was because of what they were upon. (p-70) Therefore He followed it with what indicates that it is a vain hope and a false expectation, where it is said: ﴿Do they not see﴾, meaning: do they not look so that they see ﴿that We come to the land﴾, meaning: the land of the disbelievers, ﴿reducing it from its extremities﴾. So how do they imagine that they will escape Our might? This is a representation and depiction of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, destroys of their abodes at the hands of the Muslims, and He attributes it to the abode of Islam.

﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. The fa' (then) is for denying that victory is the consequence of the reduction of the land of the disbelievers mentioned above through the Muslims' domination over it, as if it were said: the most evident of what has been mentioned and seen by them is it that their victory is imagined, as passed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾ and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Have you taken besides Him protectors?﴾. In the definite form (of "the victors") there is an allusion that the Muslims are those specifically designated for victory and known for it.

Say: "I am only warning you" after the reason for the terror of what they seek to hasten, and the extent of their wretched state when it comes, has been made clear from Him, exalted is He. Their ignorance of this, and their turning away from the remembrance of their Lord, who protects them from the calamities of night and day and from other evils of their condition, have been censured. He (ﷺ) was commanded to say to them: "I am only warning you of what you seek to hasten, the Hour, **by the revelation** (al-wahy), which is true and speaks of its coming and of the terror of its horrors." That is: my role is only to warn you by informing you of it, not by bringing it about, for that would conflict with the **creative wisdom** (al-hikma al-takwiniyya) and the **legislative wisdom** (al-hikma al-tashri'iyya), since faith is based on proof (burhani), not on direct sight (ʿayani).

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And the deaf do not hear the call﴾, it may be part of the words that were taught to him, a **concluding remark** (tadhyil) appended to them by way of **parenthetical insertion** (i'tiradh). He, peace be upon him, was commanded to say it to them as a rebuke, a reproach, and a record against them of their complete ignorance and obstinacy. The **lam** here is **lam al-jins** (the generic definite article), which includes the addressees in a primary sense, or it is **lam al-ʿahd** (the anaphoric definite article). He placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, to record against them their deafness. The negation of hearing is restricted by His saying: ﴿when they are warned﴾, although deaf people do not hear speech, whether it is a warning or good news, to show the full extent of the severity of their deafness. Likewise, the choice of "call" (du'a'), which is an expression for sound and summons, over "speech" (kalam) for this reason is significant, because a warning is usually given with loud, repeated sounds accompanied by signs that indicate it. So if they do not hear these, their deafness is at an extreme with no beyond.

Or it may be from Him, exalted is He, in the manner of His saying: ﴿But they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾. This is supported by the **recitation** (qira'a) in the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) with **al-ism'a'** (causing to hear), with the words "the deaf" and "the call" in the accusative, as if it were said: "Say to them that, while you are far from making them hear." It is also recited with the **ya'** (the third-person masculine prefix), with the subject being him, peace be upon him. It is also recited in the passive voice, meaning: no one is able to make the deaf hear.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if but a breath of your Lord's punishment should touch them﴾ is an explanation of how swiftly they are affected by the arrival of the breath of punishment, following the explanation of their lack of being affected by the arrival of its news, in the manner of an oath-based emphasis. That is: "By God, if even the slightest affliction of His punishment should reach them, even its least part," as is indicated by the touching (mass) and the breath (nafkha) in their substance and form, for the origin of nafkh (blowing) is the wafting of the scent of a thing.

﴿They will surely say: "Woe to us! Indeed we have been wrongdoers."﴾ They will call down woe and destruction upon themselves and will confess against themselves to wrongdoing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 47:

Allah's saying: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice﴾ is an explanation of what will occur when the threat they were warned of comes about; that is, We shall establish the just scales (al-mawazin, "the scales") by which the records of deeds are weighed. It was also said: "The setting up of the scales" is a metaphor for the establishment of precise reckoning and recompense in accordance with deeds. The detailed discussion of what it involves has already passed in (Surah al-A'raf). The word qist (justice) is in the singular because it is a verbal noun (masdar) described by the adjective, for emphasis (mubalaghah).

﴿for the Day of Resurrection﴾, which they used to ask to hasten, that is: for its recompense, or for the sake of its people, or within it, as in your saying: "I came on the fifth of the month" (li-khams khalawna min al-shahr).

﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ of souls, ﴿at all﴾, that is, of any of its rights, or in any manner of wrong, but every person with a right will be given his right: if it is good, then good, and if it is evil, then evil. The fa' (so) indicates that the absence of wrong follows from the setting up of the scales.

﴿And even if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾, that is, the act denoted by the setting up of the scales; ﴿We shall bring it forth﴾, that is, the quantity of a grain existing from mustard seed, meaning that even if it is at the extreme of smallness and insignificance, since the grain of mustard is a proverb for smallness. It has also been read as "mithqalu habbatin" with the nominative (raf'), taking kana as a complete (taammah) verb.

﴿We bring it forth﴾ means: We bring forth that deed, expressed by the weight of a grain of mustard, for weighing. The feminine pronoun is due to its being attached to "grain" (habbah). It has also been read "ataynā bihā" (We requited with it), from the sense of ityan meaning recompense and reward, because they brought the deeds and He brought the recompense to them. It has also been read "uthibna" (We shall reward), from thawab (reward). It has also been read "ji'na bihā" (We came with it).

﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾, since (Our knowledge and Our justice) are beyond increase.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 48:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion, and a light, and a reminder for the God-fearing.﴾ This is a kind of elaboration of what was stated in summary in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you any but men to whom We revealed...﴾ up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾. It also indicates how they were saved and how their enemies were destroyed. Introducing it with the oath of emphasis serves to show the complete care given to its content. By "the Criterion" is meant the Torah, and likewise by "the light" and "the reminder." That is, by God, We certainly gave them both a shining revelation and a book combining being a distinguisher between truth and falsehood, a light dispelling ignorance and error, and a reminder by which people may be admonished. The God-fearing are singled out for mention because they are the ones who are illuminated by its lights and who benefit from the gains of its traces, or [the reminder is] of what they need of the laws and rulings. It was said: "the Criterion" means victory; it was said: it means the splitting of the sea. The first is the one fitting to the context of this noble discourse, since it serves to confirm the matter of the Qur'an, which shares with the other divine books, especially the Torah, the attributes mentioned. Also, the splitting of the sea is what the disbelievers demanded the like of when they said: ﴿So let him bring us a sign as the earlier ones were sent [with signs].﴾ It is read: "ḍiyā'an" without the waw, as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of "al-Furqān."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 49:

As for His saying, ﴿Those who fear their Lord﴾, i.e., His punishment, it is in the genitive case (majrur al-mahall) by virtue of being a descriptive adjective (sifah madihah) for the God-conscious (al-muttaqin), or an apposition (badal), or an explanatory clarification (bayan), or in the accusative (mansub), or in the nominative (marfu') by way of praise (al-mad-h).

﴿Unseen﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object (al-maf'ul), i.e., they fear His punishment, may He be exalted, while it is unseen by them and not witnessed by them. Therein is an allusion (ta'rid) to the disbelievers, in that they are not affected by warning until they witness what they have been warned of. It is said: it is from the subject (al-fa'il).

﴿And they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾, i.e., they are fearful of it with diligent concern. The placing of the prepositional phrase first is for the sake of observing the rhyme (al-fawasil). The singling out of their apprehension of it for mention, after describing them with fear in general, serves to signal that it is the greatest of the frightening things, and to specify their possession of the opposite of what characterises those who seek to hasten it. The choice of the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) serves to indicate the constancy and continuity of the apprehension.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 50:

﴿And this﴾, i.e., the Noble Qur'an, is pointed to with "this" to signify the utmost clarity of its matter, ﴿is a reminder﴾ by which whoever seeks to be mindful is reminded (p-72). It is described by the last attribute, which is used for the Torah, for the sake of the appropriateness of the context and its agreement with what has preceded at the beginning of the noble surah. ﴿Blessed﴾: abundant in goodness, great in benefit, sought for blessing. ﴿That We have sent down﴾: either a second attribute of "reminder," or another predicate.

﴿Will you then deny it?﴾ This is a rebuke for their denial after it has become manifest, and the fact that its sending down is like the giving of the Torah, as if it were said: Is it far-fetched that you know that its matter is like the matter of the Torah in being given and revealed, and yet you deny that it has been sent down from Us? For that, after considering the state of the Torah, has no basis whatsoever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 51:

﴿And We certainly gave Abraham his right guidance﴾. That is: the rectitude (rushd) befitting him and such great messengers as him, which is the perfect guidance grounded in the special direction attained through revelation, and the capacity to reform the community by employing the divine laws (nawamis ilahiyya). It is also read "rashadahu," and the two are dialectal variants, like "al-huzn" and "al-hazan" (both meaning sorrow).

﴿from before﴾: that is, before the giving of the Torah to Moses and Aaron. The mention of its giving is placed first because of the complete resemblance between it and the sending down of the Qur'an. It has been said: before his prophethood (istinba'), or before his reaching maturity (bulugh), but the context rejects this.

﴿and We had knowledge of him﴾: that is, that he was worthy of what We had given him. In this is evidence, which is not hidden, that God Most High has knowledge of particulars and chooses freely in His acts.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 52:

﴿When he said to his father and his people﴾ is a adverbial phrase (zarf) governed by "ātaynā" (We gave), on the basis that it is an extended period of time in which the giving occurred and what was consequent upon it of his actions and sayings. It has also been said that it is an object (maf'ūl) of an implied, resumed verb which serves as a causal explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it, meaning: mention the time when he said to them: ﴿What are these images (tamāthīl) to which you are devoted?﴾ so that you may stand upon the perfection of his right guidance and the utmost of his excellence. The timthāl (image) is a name for a manufactured thing made to resemble one of the creatures of God Most High. This is a feigned ignorance on his part, peace be upon him, in that he asked them about their idols with "mā" (what), which is used to seek clarification of the reality of a thing, or he explained the name, as if he did not know what they were, despite his full awareness that their reality is stone or wood, which they took as objects of worship. He expressed their worship of them by the general term "ʿukūf" (devotion), which is a metaphor for constant adherence and persistence upon a thing for some purpose, intending thereby to belittle and humiliate them, and as a rebuke to them for their glorifying of them. The "lām" in "lahā" (to them/for them) is for specification (ikhtiṣāṣ) and not for transitivity (ta'diyah); otherwise the word "ʿalā" would have been used. The meaning is: you are the doers of devotion to them.

It has been permitted to take the verb "al-'ukuf" (devoted attachment, staying in devotion) as implying the meaning of "worship" (ibadah), as indicated by His, the Exalted, words: ﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ They answered with this because the purpose of his question, upon him be peace, was an inquiry into the reason for their worshipping them, as is indicated by his, upon him be peace, describing them as being devoted to them (al-'ukuf lahā). It is as if he had said: "What are these, do they deserve what you do of devotion to them?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 54:

When they had no tenable refuge, they resorted to imitation (taqlid, blind adherence to the authority of others). He, peace be upon him, refuted it by way of emphatic oath, where he said: ﴿He said: "Indeed you have been, you and your fathers,"﴾ who established for you this false practice, ﴿in manifest error,﴾ of a wondrous kind whose extent cannot be measured, ﴿clear.﴾ That is: evident and plain, such that its being so is hidden from no one among the people of intellect. The meaning of "you have been" is the mere continuance of their persistence in error, not a past persistence that occurred before the time of the address that encompasses them and their fathers. That is: by God, you have indeed been persisting in a great error (p-73) that is evident, because it is not supported by any proof whatsoever. And taqlid is only permissible in matters that admit of being correct in general.

They said, "Have you come to us with the truth, or are you one of those who jest?"

Here the people, on hearing his words (peace be upon him), expressed their disbelief that what they were upon could be misguidance, and their astonishment at his misleading them (peace be upon him) by way of emphatic oath, and their hesitation as to whether this came from him (peace be upon him) in earnest. ﴿Have you come to us with the truth﴾, i.e., with earnestness, ﴿or are you one of the jesters﴾, so that you say what you say by way of jest and levity. And in the expression of the last alternative as a nominal sentence, which denotes permanence, there is an indication that it is the more probable in their view.

﴿He said﴾ (peace be upon him), by way of a *idrab* (a shift away from what they had built their claim on, namely their belief that the idols were their lords, as their words reveal: ﴿We worship idols and remain devoted to them﴾). It is as if it was said: the matter is not as you think.

﴿Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them﴾. It has also been said that this is a shift away from his being a player, by establishing proof for what he claimed. The pronoun هُنَّ (*hunna*, "them") refers to the heavens and the earth. He described Himself, exalted is He, as their creator right after describing Himself as their Lord, to affirm the truth and to draw attention to the fact that whatever does not have this quality has no share in lordship. That is, He brought them into being with what is in them of created things, among which are you, your fathers, and what you worship, without any model to imitate or any pattern to follow. Returning the pronoun to the images (*tamathil*) is more effective in misleading them and more evident in establishing the proof against them, because it contains a clear statement that makes reflection unnecessary on the fact that what they worship is among created things.

﴿And I am, concerning that﴾, which I have mentioned, namely that your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth alone, to the exclusion of anything else, whatever it may be, ﴿among the witnesses﴾, that is, those who know it in reality and establish proof for it. For the one who witnesses to a thing is the one who has verified it and confirmed it, and his witnessing to it consists in presenting the argument for it and establishing it by that argument. It is as if he said: I explain that and prove it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 57:

﴿By Allah﴾ It is also read with the letter bāʾ (ب), which is the original form; the tāʾ (ت) is a substitution for the wāw (و), which is itself a substitution for the original bāʾ. In it there is an expression of wonder (taʿjīb).

﴿I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ That is: I will certainly exert myself to break them. In it is an announcement of the difficulty of seizing the opportunity and of its dependence on the use of stratagems. He, peace be upon him, said this in secret, and it has been said that only one man heard it.

﴿after you have turned away, retreating﴾ from your worship of them to your festival. It is also read as "tawallaw" (تَوَلَّوْا), from the verb tawallī, with one of the two tāʾs elided, and his words, exalted is He, support this reading: ﴿so they turned away from him, retreating﴾.

The fa' in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So he made them﴾, is fasihah (an elliptical fa', indicating an implied clause), meaning: they turned away, so he made them ﴿judhadhan﴾, that is, fragments. Fu'al here is in the sense of maf'ul (passive), from al-jadhdh (cutting), which is al-qat' (cutting off), like hutam (debris) from al-hatm (breaking), which is al-kasr (breaking). It is also read with a kasra (jidhadhan), and this is a dialect; or it is the plural of jadhidh, like khifaf and khafif. It is also read with a fatha (jadhadhan). And judhudhan is the plural of jadhidh, and judhadhan is the plural of juddah.

It is narrated that Azar took him out on one of their festival days, and they began with the house of the idols, entered it, prostrated to them, and placed food among them, which they had brought with them, saying: "Until the gods bless our food with its blessing, when we return." Then they departed, and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) remained behind. He looked at the idols, and they were seventy idols arranged in rows, and there was a great idol facing the door, which was made of gold, and in its eyes were two jewels that shone at night. So he broke them all with an axe that was in his hand, and left none but the largest, and he hung the axe around its neck. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except a large one among them﴾, that is, for the idols, ﴿so that they might return to it﴾, that is, to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), ﴿and question him﴾, so he would argue with them by what will come, and confound and silence them. It has been said: they return to the large one and ask it about the breaker, because it is part of the nature of a deity that people turn to it in calamities. It has also been said: they return to God Exalted and to His unity, when they realize the helplessness of their gods in repelling what befalls them and in harming the one who broke them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 59:

﴿They said﴾ — that is, when they returned from their festival and saw what they saw — ﴿"Who has done this to our gods?"﴾ in the manner of denunciation, reproach and outrage. They expressed it with what was mentioned, and did not point to them with "these" while they were before them, for the sake of intensifying the outrage. As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿"Indeed, he is among the wrongdoers"﴾, it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it. It has been said that "man" (من) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and this sentence is in the place of nominative case (raf') as its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: the one who did this breaking and smashing to our gods — indeed he is counted among the wrongdoers, either for his audacity in humiliating them, though they are deserving of reverence, or for his excess in breaking and smashing and his persistence in belittling them, or by exposing himself to destruction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 60:

﴿They said﴾: that is, some of them, answering the questioners. ﴿"We heard a youth mention them"﴾: that is, disparage them, so perhaps he did this to them. The words of His, exalted is He, "mention them" (yadhkuruhum) are either a second object of "heard" (sami'a) because it relates to the thing itself, or a qualifier of "youth" (fata) that makes its relation to it valid. This is when those who said it heard him, peace be upon him, personally mentioning them. If they had only heard from people that he, peace be upon him, mentioned them with evil, then there is no need for a qualifier that makes it valid.

﴿"Called Abraham"﴾: another qualifier of "youth" (fata), that is, this name is applied to him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 61:

﴿They said﴾ That is: the questioners. ﴿"Then bring him before the eyes of the people"﴾ That is: in sight of them, in such a place that he is set before their eyes on an elevated spot, so that he is hardly hidden from anyone. ﴿"That perhaps they may bear witness"﴾ That is: that they may be present at our punishment of him. It has also been said: "that perhaps they may bear witness to his deed or to his saying that," and in that case the pronoun does not refer to "the people" but to some unspecified or known group among them.

Qur'an 21:62 — "They said:" — This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) responding to a question arising from the narration of their words, as if it were said: "What did they then do with him, peace be upon him, after that? Did they bring him first?" It is answered: "They brought him, then they said: ﴿Are you the one who did this to our gods, O Ibrahim?﴾" The narration is limited to their address to him, peace be upon him, to draw attention to the fact that their bringing him and their hastening to that is a certain matter, independent of explanation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 21, verse 63:**

﴿He said: "Rather, this one, their chief, did it."﴾ Pointing to the one who had not broken them, he (peace be upon him) took an allusive (*ta'ridi*) course that would lead to his objective, which was to establish the proof against them in the most gentle and fitting manner, by directing them to reflect on the matter of their gods. This also avoided lying. He presented the big idol as the one who spoke in the context of being directly responsible for the act by attributing it to him. He presented it in the same allusive manner as an act that puts the axe on its neck. He intended to attribute the act to it by way of causation (*tasbib*), since those idols had angered him, peace be upon him, when he saw them lined up in order for worship besides God, glorified is He. The anger of their chief was greater and more intense according to the increase in their veneration of him. So he attributed the act to him on the basis that he was the one who prompted it.

It is also said: this is a report of what leads to the permissibility of their own position, as if he had said to them: "Why do you deny that their chief could have done it? For whoever is worshipped and called a god ought to be able to do what is even more difficult than that."

It is related that he (peace be upon him) said: "Their chief did this; he was angry that these lesser ones were worshipped along with him while he is greater than them." This would be an illustration by which he, peace be upon him, intended to alert them to the wrath of God, exalted is He, upon them for associating others with His worship by worshipping idols.

As for what has been said, that he, peace be upon him, did not intend to attribute the act that proceeded from him to the big idol, but rather intended only to affirm it for himself and establish it for himself in an allusive style, through which he achieved his purpose of establishing the proof against them and rebuking them, and he illustrated this with the case of someone who says to you, an unlettered person, about something you have written in an elegant hand, while you are famous for beautiful handwriting: "Did you write this?" and you reply to him: "Rather, you wrote it." Your intention would be to affirm the writing for yourself, together with mocking the questioner by denying it of yourself and affirming it for him. This is far from verification (*tahqiq*), because the essence of the meaning in the mentioned example is merely affirming the writing for oneself, claiming that the matter is evident, mocking the questioner, and showing his ignorance in asking, since his question is based on the supposition that its issuing from someone other than you is possible in his view, while it is impossible in yours. There is no doubt that what he, peace be upon him, meant by attributing the breaking to the idol was not merely affirming it for himself, nor showing their ignorance in their question, which is based on the possibility of its issuing from another in their view. Rather, what he, peace be upon him, meant was to direct them toward reflection on the condition of their idols, as his saying indicates: ﴿So ask them, if they can speak.﴾ That is, if they are of the kind that can speak. He did not say "if they can hear or understand," even though asking also depends on hearing and understanding, because the outcome of a question is the answer, and their inability to speak is more evident, and rebuking them with it is more effective.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 64:

This occurred first, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they turned back to themselves﴾, that is: they reflected with their minds and remembered that what cannot ward off harm from itself, nor retaliate against the one who broke it in any way, is impossible to be able to ward off harm from others or bring benefit to them. So how could it deserve to be worshipped?

﴿Then they said﴾, that is: some of them said to others among themselves, ﴿Indeed, you are the wrongdoers﴾, that is: by this questioning, for it was in the manner of rebuke that entails accountability; or by worshipping idols, not by the one who wronged them by your saying, "He is among the wrongdoers"; or you are wrongdoers by worshipping them, not the one who broke them.

﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads﴾ That is: they turned back to disputation after they had stood firm through the review (of their argument). He likened their return to falsehood to the situation in which the lower part of a thing becomes its upper part.

It is also read "nukkisū" with the doubled letter (tashdid), and "nakkasū" in the active voice, meaning: they overturned themselves.

﴿Indeed you know that these do not speak﴾ This is on the supposition of a saying, meaning: saying, "By God, you indeed know that speech is not among their capacities, so how do you order us to ask them?" Moreover, the intended meaning is the continuation of the negation of speech, not the negation of its continuation, as the form of the present tense might suggest.

(p-76) ﴿He said﴾, rebuking them: ﴿Do you then worship﴾, that is, do you know this and yet worship ﴿besides Allah﴾, that is, going beyond worshipping Him, the Exalted, ﴿what neither benefits you in anything﴾ of benefit ﴿nor harms you﴾. For knowledge of its state, which is incompatible with divinity, is among the things that necessarily require abstaining from worshipping it, definitely.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 67:

﴿Fie upon you, and upon what you worship besides Allah!﴾ This is an expression of exasperation on his part, peace be upon him, at their persistence in manifest falsehood. The use of the noble Name (Allah) in the place where a pronoun could have been used serves to further emphasize the ugliness of what they did. "Uff" (أُفٍّ) is the sound made by one who is exasperated, and its meaning is: ugliness and foulness. The lam (اللام) indicates the one for whom the expression of disgust is made.

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ That is: Will you not reflect, so that you would understand (تَعْقِلُونَ) the ugliness of your action?

﴿They said﴾, that is, some of them said to one another, when they were unable to argue and their stratagems were exhausted and their pretexts failed them. This is the habit of the defeated falsifier: when you strike his doubt with a decisive proof and he is exposed, he has no recourse left but hostility.

﴿Burn him﴾, for it is the most severe of punishments. ﴿And support your gods﴾ by avenging them ﴿if you are going to act﴾, that is, to give support, or to do something that counts. It is said that the speaker was Nimrod ibn Kan'an ibn al-Sanjarib ibn Nimrod ibn Kush ibn Ham ibn Nuh. It is also said that he was a man from the Kurds of Fars named Hayun, and it is said that he was Hadir, whom the earth swallowed. It is reported that when they resolved to burn him, peace be upon him, they built for him an enclosure at Kutha, a village among the villages of the Anbat. This is His Exalted saying: ﴿They said: Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire.﴾ They gathered hard firewood of various kinds for a period of forty days and kindled a great fire, so that no one could come near it. Even a bird passing over it at the highest part of the air would be burned by the intensity of its heat. No one could approach it, so they did not know how to cast him into it, peace be upon him. Then Iblis came to them and taught them how to make the manjaniq (catapult), and they made it. It is also said that a man from the Kurds made it for them, and God Most High caused the earth to swallow him, and he continues to sink into it until the Day of Resurrection. Then they set upon Abraham, peace be upon him, and bound him in chains and cast him into it. Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." He said: "Then ask your Lord." He said: "My knowledge of my condition is sufficient for me as a request."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 69:

By the blessing of His word, God Most High made the enclosure a garden. This is His saying, Most High: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾ That is, "Be possessed of coolness and safety," i.e., "Cool down with a coolness that does no harm." In this there are several intensifications: the making of the fire, which is subjugated to His power, into something commanded and obedient; the placing of "be coolness" in the position of "cool down"; then the omission of the modified noun (mudaf) and the placing of the modifier (mudaf ilayhi) in its stead. It has also been said that "salaman" is in the accusative governed by a verb of its own, meaning: "and We greeted him with a greeting of peace." It is narrated that the angels took hold of Abraham by his upper arms and seated him on the ground, and behold, there was a spring of sweet water, red roses, and narcissus, and the fire burned nothing but his bonds. It is also narrated that he, peace be upon him, remained in it for forty or fifty days, and said: "I was never in a more pleasant state of life than when I was in it." Ibn Yasar said: God Most High sent the angel of shade, who sat by his side to keep him company. Nimrod looked out from his palace, came to the edge, and saw him sitting in a delightful garden, with a companion sitting beside him in the best of forms, while the fire surrounded him. He called out, "O Abraham, are you able to come out of it?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then get up and come out." So he rose, walking, and came out of it. Nimrod met him, honored him, and said: "Who is the man whom I saw with you?" He said: "That is the angel of shade, whom my Lord sent to keep me company." Nimrod said: "I will offer a sacrifice to your Lord for what I have seen of His power and might in what He did to you." He, peace be upon him, said: "God will not accept anything from you as long as you remain upon this religion of yours." He said: "I cannot abandon my kingship, but I will slaughter for Him four thousand cows," and he slaughtered them and withheld from Abraham, peace be upon him. At that time he was sixteen years old. This, as you see, is among the most wondrous of miracles, for the transformation of fire into pleasant air, though it is not an innovation from the power of God, the Mighty and Majestic, yet the occurrence of that in this form is among what breaks customary norms.

It is also said: the fire remained as it was, but the Exalted (Allah) warded off its harm from him, peace be upon him, as you see in the salamander (al-samandal), as the apparent sense of His saying, the Exalted, concerning Abraham indicates: ﴿And they intended a plot against him﴾, a great scheme to harm him, ﴿but We made them the greatest losers﴾, i.e., the greatest loser of all losers, since their effort to extinguish the light of truth turned into a decisive proof that he, peace be upon him, was upon the truth while they were upon falsehood, and into a cause for raising his rank and for their deserving the most severe punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 71:

﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds.﴾ That is: from Iraq to Syria (al-Sham). Its general blessings are that most of the prophets were sent within it, so their laws (shara'i') spread throughout the worlds, and these laws are the foundations (mabadi') of perfections and goods, both religious and worldly. It was also said: abundance of bounties and generally plentiful produce. It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) alighted in Palestine, while Lot (peace be upon him) was at al-Mu'tafikah, and between them was a distance of a day and a night's journey.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 72:

﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as a gift (nafilah)﴾. That is: a bounty, so it is in a state of being a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of both of them; or it is a son; or it is an addition over what he asked for, which was Isaac, so it is specific to Jacob, and there is no ambiguity in it because of the apparent indication (al-qarinah al-zahirah).

﴿And each of them﴾, that is, each one of these four, not some of them to the exclusion of others, ﴿We made righteous (salihin)﴾, by granting them success in righteousness in religion and in worldly affairs, so they became perfect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 73:

﴿And We made them imams﴾ who are followed in matters of religion, in answer to his prayer, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿And of my offspring﴾.

﴿Guiding﴾, i.e., the community, to the truth ﴿by Our command﴾ to them in this, and by Our sending them, until they became perfecters (of themselves and others).

﴿And We inspired in them the doing of good deeds﴾ so that they would urge others to it, and thus their perfection would be complete by joining action to knowledge. Its original form is "that you do good deeds, then the doing of good deeds" (an ʿaṭf of the same kind, i.e., the verbal noun ﴿fiʿl﴾ being in apposition to the verb form). Likewise is the Exalted One's saying: ﴿and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat﴾, which is ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm (the mention of the particular after the general) to indicate their excellence and eminence. The tāʾ of ﴿iqāmah﴾ (in place of the verbal noun) was dropped, being the compensatory tāʾ replacing one of the two alifs, because the genitive noun that follows it (i.e., ﴿ṣalāh﴾) takes its place.

﴿And they were worshippers of Us﴾, specifically and not of anyone else, ﴿worshipping﴾, with no thought in their minds other than worship of Us.

(p-78) ﴿And Lot⦆ It is said: he is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb which is explained by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿We gave him﴾, meaning: and We gave Lot. It is also said: (the verb is) "mention" (udhkur).

﴿Judgment⦆ meaning: wisdom, or prophethood, or the decision between disputants with truth; ﴿and knowledge⦆ of what it befits the prophets, peace be upon them, to know.

﴿And We delivered him from the town that used to do the vile deeds⦆ meaning: sodomy (al-liwat). The town is described with the attribute of its people and that attribute is ascribed to it, by eliding the genitive noun (mudaf) and placing the town in its position, as His words, Exalted is He, indicate: ﴿Indeed they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient⦆, for it serves as a reason for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 75:

﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy﴾ i.e., among the people of Our mercy, or into Our Paradise (jannah). ﴿Indeed, he was among the righteous (salihin)﴾ who had already been preceded by the best (al-husna) from Us.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 76:

﴿And Noah﴾: That is, remember Noah, i.e., his story. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿when he called out﴾: that is, he invoked Allah, exalted is He, against his people for their destruction. (This) is an adverbial clause (zarf) governing the implied genitive noun (mudaf muqaddar), i.e., remember his account that took place at the time of his supplication ﴿before﴾: that is, before these mentioned ones.

﴿So We answered him﴾: that is, his supplication, of which his saying is part: ﴿that I am overcome, so help (me)﴾.

﴿And We delivered him and his family from the great distress﴾, which is the flood. It was also said: the harm inflicted by his people. The root meaning of karb (distress) is intense grief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 77:

﴿And We helped him﴾ with a help that entailed retribution and victory. For this reason it was said: ﴿against the people who denied Our signs﴾. Taking it to mean "so he avenged himself" (fa-ntasara) is rejected by what was mentioned of his supplication, peace be upon him, for its apparent sense requires attributing the victory to Him, the Exalted, together with what this carries of magnifying the matter. The Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil﴾ is a justification for what precedes it and a preparation for what follows it, namely the Exalted's saying: ﴿so We drowned them all﴾, for persistence in denying the truth and immersion in evil and corruption is, beyond doubt, something that necessitates destruction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 78:

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾: either it is conjoined to ﴿Nuh﴾ (the object of the same verb as its governing element), or it is conjoined to a suppressed element coordinated with that governing verb, with an elided noun (mudaf) assumed. The statement of the Exalted, ﴿when they judged﴾, is a temporal clause (zarf) governing the assumed elided noun, and the use of the present tense (mudari') is a narration of a past state in order to bring its image to mind; that is, mention their account at the time of their judgment ﴿concerning the tilth﴾, i.e., concerning the crop, or the vineyard whose trellis had fallen down, as has been said, or it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from both of them.

The statement of the Exalted, ﴿when the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾, i.e., scattered and spread out ﴿into it﴾ at night without a shepherd, so they grazed it and destroyed it, is a temporal clause (zarf) for the judgment.

﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, i.e., to the judgment of the judges and of those who submitted to their ruling, for the annexation (idafa) is for mere specification, which encompasses the specification of the standing and the specification of the occurrence. It is also read: ﴿to their judgment﴾ [in the dual, referring to the two of them].

﴿witnesses﴾: present in knowledge. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) that confirms the judgment and conveys greater attention to its matter.

(p-79)﴿So We gave Solomon the understanding of it﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "yahkumān" (they judged), since it has the sense of the past tense. It is also read "fa-afhamnāhā" (﴿So We made Solomon understand it﴾). The pronoun refers either to the judgment (ḥukūma) or to the verdict (fatwā).

It is reported that two men entered upon Dawud, peace be upon him. One of them said: "This man's sheep entered my field at night and ruined it." So he ruled for him with the sheep. The two went out and passed by Sulayman, peace be upon him, and informed him of this. He said: "Other than this is gentler on both parties." Dawud heard him and summoned him, and said to him: "By the right of sonship and fatherhood, tell me what is gentler on both parties." He said: "I see that the sheep should be handed over to the owner of the land, so that he benefits from their milk, offspring and wool, and the field should be handed over to the owners of the sheep, so that they may tend it until it returns to what it was, and then they exchange back." He said: "The judgment is what you have judged," and he enforced the ruling accordingly.

What I hold is that their ruling, peace be upon them both, was based on ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning). Sulayman's statement "other than this is gentler on both parties," and then his statement "I see that it should be handed over…," are clear evidence that it was not by way of revelation. Otherwise he would have pronounced the verdict definitively, and Dawud, peace be upon them both, would not have adjured him to reveal what he had. Rather, it would have been obligatory for him to disclose it from the outset, or forbidden for him to conceal it. It follows necessarily that the earlier judgment was also of this kind, because a textual ruling cannot be overturned by ijtihad. Rather, I say, and God Most High knows best: Sulayman's opinion was istihsān (juristic preference, choosing what is considered more equitable over a strict analogy), as his saying "gentler on both parties" indicates, and Dawud's opinion was qiyas (analogical reasoning). This is like the case where a slave commits an offense against a person: according to Abu Hanifa, the master hands him over to the injured party, or else ransoms him and sells him to pay for it; according to al-Shafi'i, the master ransoms him. It has been reported that there was no difference between the value of the field and the value of the sheep.

As for Sulayman, peace be upon him, he exercised istihsān when he made the benefit from the sheep correspond to the benefit lost from the field, without the owner's ownership of the sheep being removed. He also obligated the owner of the sheep to work on the field until the harm caused by his animals was repaired. This is like what the followers of al-Shafi'i said about one who seized (ghasb) a slave and he then absconded from him: he is liable for the value, and the one from whom it was seized benefits from that value in return for the benefits the usurper deprived him of. When the runaway is found, they exchange back.

In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We gave Solomon the understanding of it﴾, there is evidence for the preference of his opinion, and that Dawud, peace be upon him, returned to it. Yet a judgment based on ijtihad is overturned by another ijtihad, even if the latter is stronger, because that is one of the distinctive features of our Shariʿa. Moreover, it is reported in the traditions that Dawud, peace be upon him, had not finalized the judgment in that matter until he heard what he heard from Sulayman.

As for the rule of this case in our Shariʿa: according to Abu Hanifa, may God Most High have mercy on him, there is no liability if there is no driver or leader with the animals; according to al-Shafi'i, liability is due at night but not during the day.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ is to remove what might be suggested by singling out Sulayman, peace be upon him, for the understanding, namely that Dawud's judgment was not a legal ruling (ḥukm sharʿī). That is, each of the two of them We gave judgment and abundant knowledge, not Sulayman alone. This only indicates that the error of a mujtahid (one qualified to exercise ijtihad) does not disqualify him from being a mujtahid. It has been said, however, that it indicates that every mujtahid is correct (muṣīb). This is contrary to His saying: ﴿So We gave Solomon the understanding of it﴾. Were it not for the transmitted report, it would be possible that their two positions agree, and that His saying ﴿So We gave Solomon the understanding of it﴾ was to show what He bestowed upon him in his youth, for he, peace be upon him, was then eleven years old.

﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] along with David﴾ begins an explanation of what is specific to each of the two of them of His honor, Exalted is He, after the explanation of His general honor bestowed on both. ﴿Glorifying﴾, that is, sanctifying God, Mighty and Majestic, along with him, with a voice that takes form for him, or God Most High creates speech in them. It has been said: they traveled with him by swimming (sibāḥa), and this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the mountains, or a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) explaining the manner of the subjection. "Maʿa" (along with) is connected to the subjection. It has been said that it is connected to the glorifying, but this is distant.

﴿And the birds﴾ is a conjunction upon the mountains, or an object in the sense of "together with" (maʿa). It is also read in the nominative, on the basis of inception (ibtidāʾ), with the predicate omitted, that is, "and the birds are subjected." It has been said that it is a conjunction upon the pronoun in "yasbaḥna" (they glorify), but this is weak, because there is no emphasis and no separation.

﴿And We were ever doers﴾, that is: it is part of Our practice to do the like of it. So it is no novelty from Us, even if it is novel in your sight.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 80:

﴿And We taught him the craft of making coats of mail﴾, i.e., the making of the armour (al-dir'), and labbus (labus) in its original sense means clothing.

The one who said it:

؎ Wear for every circumstance its garment, whether its comfort or its hardship

It is also said: they were plates, and he (David) linked and wove them together. ﴿for you﴾ is connected to "We taught," or to an omitted word which is a qualifier of labus.

﴿to protect you﴾, i.e., the labus, by interpretation as "armour." It was also read with the masculine pronoun (lituhsinakum as liyuhsinakum), on the basis that the pronoun refers to Dawud, peace be upon him, or to "al-labus." It was also read with the first-person plural of majesty (linuhsinakum). In that reading it is a substitution of part (badal ishtimal) for "for you," with the preposition repeated, explaining the manner of the particularity and the benefit derived from the lam in "for you."

﴿from your violence﴾. It has been said: from the war of your enemy; and it has been said: from the impact of weapons upon you.

﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ This is an imperative expressed in the form of a question, for emphasis or for rebuke.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 81:

﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind﴾. That is: We subjected the wind to him. The placing of the particle "lam" here, unlike its use in the first case, serves to indicate the difference between the two acts of subjugation. For the subjugation of the wind and other things that he (peace be upon him) commanded was by way of complete submission to him, obedience to his command and prohibition, and being subdued beneath his dominion. As for the subjugation of the mountains and the birds to Dawud (peace be upon him), it was not of this degree, but rather by way of following him (peace be upon him) and emulating him in the worship of Allah, Mighty and Exalted.

﴿Violent﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying "the wind," and the governing element within it is the implied verb, meaning: We subjected the wind to him while it was violent in its blowing, in that it would carry his throne far away within a short span of time, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course was a month's journey﴾. Yet in itself it was gentle and pleasant. It is also said: it was gentle at times and violent at other times, according to his (peace be upon him) will. It was also read as "al-rih" (the wind) in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), with the fronted adverbial phrase as the predicate (khabar), and "violent" is then a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the predicate, the governing element being the sense of settledness contained within it. It was also read as "al-riyah" (the winds) in both the accusative and the nominative.

﴿Running by His command﴾, that is, by His will, is a second circumstantial clause, or a substitute (badal) for the first, or a circumstantial clause from its pronoun.

﴿To the land which We have blessed﴾, and it is Syria, [carrying him] in the evening after he had set out with it in the morning. Al-Kalbi said: Solomon (peace be upon him) and his people would ride upon it from Istakhr to Syria, and wherever he wished, and then return to his dwelling.

﴿And We were Knowing of all things﴾, so that We recompense him as wisdom requires.

And from the devils (We subjected to him) those who dive for him into the seas and extract for him its precious things. It was also said that "man" (مَن) is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence, with its predicate being what precedes it; the first view is the more apparent.

﴿And other work beside that﴾, that is, other than what has been mentioned, such as building cities and palaces and inventing wondrous crafts, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries, statues...﴾ [Qur'an 34:13], and so on. Whether these are the first group or others, it is due to the generality of the word "man" (مَن), as if it were said: "and whoever they work." The pronoun referring back to it is in the plural in view of its meaning, after its scope was narrowed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from the devils﴾. It is related that those subjected to him, peace be upon him, were their disbelievers (p-81), not their believers, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from the devils﴾.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We were its guardians﴾, that is, from deviating from His command or corrupting [affairs] in accordance with what their nature requires. It was said: He appointed over them a group of angels and a group of believing jinn. Al-Zajjaj said: He used to preserve them from undoing what they had done, and their custom was to undo by night what they had done by day.

﴿وَأيُّوبَ﴾ The discussion of it is as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَداوُدَ وسُلَيْمانَ﴾. That is: "And mention the account of Ayyub (Job)," ﴿إذْ نادى رَبَّهُ أنِّي﴾, that is, "that I," ﴿مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ﴾ ("harm has touched me"). It is also read with a kasra (*Innī*), on the basis of an implied verb of saying (*iḍmār al-qawl*, the omission of "saying"), or on the basis of treating the call (*nidā'*) as carrying its meaning (*taḍmīn*, the implicit sense of a verb). *Al-ḍurr* (harm) is general to every kind of harm, while with a damma (*ḍurr*) it is specific to what affects the self, such as sickness, emaciation and the like.

﴿وَأنْتَ أرْحَمُ الرّاحِمِينَ﴾ He, exalted is He, is described with the utmost mercy after he mentioned himself with what necessitates it, and he was content with that instead of stating the request, out of gentleness in asking. He, peace be upon him, was a Roman, of the descendants of Esau (*ʿĪṣ*), son of Isaac (*Isḥāq*). God, exalted is He, tested him, and his family and wealth increased. Then God afflicted him by the destruction of his children when a house collapsed upon them, and the loss of his wealth. The sickness was in his body for eighteen years, or thirteen years, or seven years and seven months and seven days and seven hours.

It is related that his wife, Mākhīr daughter of Mīshā son of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, or Raḥmah daughter of Ifrāyim son of Yūsuf, said to him one day: "If only you would supplicate God, exalted is He." He said: "How long was the period of ease?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "I am ashamed before God, exalted is He, to ask Him, when the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease."

It is also related that Iblīs came to her in a great form and said: "I am the god of the earth. I did to your husband what I did because he abandoned me and worshipped the god of the heavens. If he prostrated to me a single prostration, I would return to him and to you all that I took from you both." In another narration: "If you prostrated to me a single prostration, I would restore the wealth and the child, and cure your wife." So she returned to Ayyub, who was cast on the dunghill (*al-Kunāsa*), and no one approached him. She informed him of the story. He, peace be upon him, said: "It seems you have been tempted by the words of the accursed. If God, mighty and majestic, restores my health, I will strike you a hundred lashes, and it is forbidden for me to taste any of your food or drink after this." So he drove her away. He remained lying on the dunghill, with no one from the people approaching him. At that point he fell prostrate and said: "My Lord, harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." It was said to him: "Raise your head, for We have answered you. Strike with your foot." So he struck, and a spring of water gushed from beneath him. He bathed in it, and no creature remained on the outward part of his body but fell off, and no wound but healed. Then he struck a second time, and another spring gushed forth, and he drank from it, and no disease remained in his inner body but it left, and he returned healthy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 84:

His youth and his beauty returned to him, and then he was clothed in a robe. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We answered him and removed what was afflicting him of harm﴾. When he stood up he began to look around, and he saw nothing that had belonged to him of family and wealth except that Allah, exalted is He, had multiplied it. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. It has been said: that was by his having born to him twice what he had had.

Then his wife said to herself: "Suppose he has driven me away; shall I leave him until he dies of hunger and the beasts devour him? I will return to him." So when she returned, she did not see that dunghill nor that condition, and the affairs had changed. She began to go around the place where the dunghill had been, weeping, and she was too awed to approach the owner of the robe and ask about him. So Ayyub sent for her and called her, and said: "What do you want, O servant of Allah?" She wept and said: "I want that afflicted man who used to be lying on the dunghill." He said to her: "What became of him?" She wept and said: "My husband." He said: "Would you recognize him if you saw him?" She said: "Could he be hidden from me?" Then he smiled, and said: "I am that one." So she recognized him by his laughter and embraced him.

﴿A mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers﴾. That is: We gave him what was mentioned, as a mercy from Us to Ayyub, and as a reminder to others of the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient and be rewarded as he was rewarded. Or it means: a mercy from Us to the worshippers, among whom is Ayyub, and Our remembrance of them with goodness and Our not forgetting them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 85:

﴿And Isma'il, and Idris, and Dhu al-Kifl﴾. That is: remember them. Dhu al-Kifl (the one of the kifl) is Ilyas. It is also said that he is Yusha' ibn Nun, and it is also said that he is Zakariyya. He was named so because he had a portion (hazz) from God, Exalted, or because he took on (takaffala) a responsibility from Him, or (he had) double ( d'if) the deed and reward of the prophets of his time. For the word kifl comes in the sense of portion (nasib), guarantee (kafala), and doubling (did'f).

﴿Each of them﴾, that is, each one of these ﴿is among the patient﴾, that is, patient over the hardships of the obligations and the severity of calamities. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), coming as an answer to a question arising from the command to mention them.

And We admitted them into Our mercy (﴿وَأدْخَلْناهم في رَحْمَتِنا﴾). That is, into prophethood, or into the blessing of the Hereafter (﴿إنَّهم مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾), that is: they were among those perfect in righteousness, the complete righteousness around which no taint of corruption hovers. They are the prophets, for their righteousness is protected from the turbidity of corruption.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 87:

﴿And Dhu al-Nun﴾ That is: remember the companion of the fish, who is Yunus (peace be upon him), ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ That is: defiant toward his people, when he grew weary of their long-lasting call to them, the severity of their obstinacy, and the persistence of their insistence, departing from them as an emigrant before being commanded to do so. It is also said: he had promised them punishment, but it did not come to them at the appointed time because they repented, and he did not know the state of affairs, so he thought that they had lied to him, and he became angry at that. This form (mughalabah, "contending") is for emphasis; or because he angered them by emigrating, since they feared that punishment would befall them when he left. It is also read: "mughdaban" (angered).

﴿So he thought that We would not decree against him﴾ That is: We would not constrict him, or We would not decree against him with punishment, from qadar (decree); what supports this is that it is read with the doubled letter (qaddara). Or: We would not exercise Our power over him. It is also said: this is a figurative depiction of his state by the state of one who thinks that We will not have power over him, meaning: We treat him as one who thinks that We will have no power over him in his defiance of his people without awaiting Our command, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal﴾, meaning: We treat him as one who thinks that. It is also said: it was a satanic suggestion that came to his mind, and it was called "thought" for emphasis. It is read with the ya' (yaqdira, "He would not decree"), both lightened and doubled, and in both the active and passive voices.

﴿Then he called out﴾ The fa' is explanatory (fasihah), meaning: when what happened of the lot-casting and the swallowing by the fish occurred, then he called out ﴿in the darknesses﴾ That is: in the intense, dense darkness, or in the darknesses of the fish's belly, the sea, and the night. It is also said: a larger fish swallowed his fish, so he was in the darkness of the two fishes' bellies, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the night.

﴿That there is no god but You﴾ That is: that there is no god but You, where "an" is a lightened form of "inna" with the pronoun of the matter omitted; or, meaning: there is no god but You, where it is explanatory.

﴿Glory be to You﴾ I declare You far above, a declaration fitting to You, that anything could incapacitate You, or that my trial with this would have occurred without cause on my part. ﴿Indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ against their own souls, by exposing them to destruction, in that I hastened to emigrate.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 88:

﴿So We answered him﴾, that is, his supplication, which he made within the acknowledgment of his wrongdoing, in the most gentle and finest manner. From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "There is no distressed person who calls upon Allah with this supplication except that it is answered for him."

﴿And We delivered him from the distress﴾ by means of his being cast by the fish onto the shore after four hours during which he was in its belly. It was said: after three days. It was also said: the distress was the distress of being swallowed, and it was said: it was the sin.

﴿And thus﴾, that is, like that complete deliverance, ﴿We deliver the believers﴾ from distresses in which they call upon Allah Most High with sincerity, with no lesser deliverance than that. In the Imam (the 'Uthmanic codex) it is "najja", so the majority of readers suppressed the second nun, since it is suppressed before the letters of the mouth. It was also read with the jim doubled (nujjī, "nunajjī"), on the basis that its original form was "nunajjī", and the second was elided, just as the taa' was elided in tazahharun (taẓāharūn). Although the elided letter here is a fa' (a root letter), its elision is more fitting than the elision of the letter of the present tense that carries a meaning. The difference in the vowels of the two nuns does not detract from this, since the motive for elision is the coming together of two like letters together with the impossibility of assimilation, and the elision is avoided in tatajafa (tatajāfā) for fear of ambiguity. It was said: it is a passive past verb, attributed to the pronoun of the verbal noun and its final letter was made quiescent for lightness, but this was rejected on the grounds that it cannot be attributed to the verbal noun while the object is mentioned, and the past tense does not take quiescence at its end.

﴿And Zakariyya﴾, i.e., recall his account, ﴿when he called upon his Lord﴾ and said, ﴿"My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan)"﴾, i.e., solitary, without a son to inherit from me, ﴿"and You are the best of inheritors"﴾. So You suffice me if You do not grant me an heir.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 90:

﴿So We answered him﴾, i.e., his supplication, ﴿and We granted him Yahya﴾. The explanation of the manner of the answering and the granting has already passed in Surat Maryam.

﴿And We made his wife fit for him﴾, i.e., We made her fit for childbearing after her barrenness, or We made her fit for marital companionship by improving her character, and she had been ill-tempered (ḥaredah).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good deeds﴾ is a causal explanation for the various forms of His beneficence, may He be exalted, that were related to the prophets mentioned, i.e., they would hasten toward the various kinds of good while remaining firm and steadfast in the essence of goodness. This is the secret behind the choice of the word "fi" (in) over "ila" (to), which would convey the opposite of the intended meaning, namely that they were outside the essence of goodness, turning toward it, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden﴾.

﴿And they called upon Us with longing and fear﴾, meaning possessing longing and fear, or longing for reward and hoping for response, or in obedience and fearing punishment, or in disobedience, or for longing and fear.

﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾, i.e., lowly, supplicating, or constantly fearful. The meaning is that they attained from Allah, may He be exalted, what they attained because of their being characterized by these praiseworthy qualities.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 91:

﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾. That is: mention the report of her who guarded her chastity absolutely, from the lawful and the unlawful. The expression of her by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) serves to magnify her status and to declare her free from what they alleged against her, [she being] the most pure of the pure (āthar dhī athīr). ﴿So We breathed into her﴾, that is: We brought Jesus to life in her womb, ﴿of Our spirit﴾, of the spirit which is of Our command. It has been said: We caused the breathing into her by means of Our spirit, Gabriel (peace be upon him).

﴿And We made her and her son﴾, that is: their story or their state, ﴿a sign for the worlds﴾. For whoever contemplates their condition realises the perfection of the power of Him, Mighty and Majestic. Thus the meaning of "sign" is the complete sign that resulted from the two of them, together with the multiplicity of signs in each one of them. It has been said: by "sign" is meant the genus, encompassing the independent signs that each of them possesses. It has also been said: the meaning is: "We made her a sign, and her son a sign," the first being omitted because the second indicates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 92:

﴿Indeed, this﴾ i.e., the religion of tawhid (monotheism) and Islam. It is indicated by "this" to draw attention to the complete clarity of its matter in soundness and rectitude.

﴿is your community﴾ i.e., your religion (millah), which you must guard within its limits, observe its rights, and not neglect any part of it. The address is to all people without exception.

﴿one community﴾ is in the accusative of circumstance (hal) from "your community," meaning: not differing among the prophets, peace be upon them, since there is no other religion that shares in the validity of following it, nor any possibility of its being changed or altered, like the subsidiary rulings of the shari'ahs (furu' al-shara'i') which change according to the changing of nations and eras. It has also been read as "ummatakum" in the accusative as an apposition (badal) to the subject of "inna" (indeed), and "ummatun wahidatun" in the nominative as the predicate (khabar). Both have also been read in the nominative, as two predicates.

﴿And I am your Lord﴾ there is no god for you other than Me, ﴿so worship Me﴾ exclusively, and no other.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they cut their affair into pieces among themselves﴾ is a shift (iltifat) to the third person, in order to reproach them for what they corrupted of the religion through division, and for making their affair into scattered fragments, and to hand over the ugly deeds they committed to others, as if it were said: Do you not see the great thing these people have committed against the religion of God, upon which all the Prophets, peace be upon them, were agreed? ﴿Each﴾ means: each one of the divided sects, or each individual among the members of each of those sects.

﴿To Us they will return﴾ by resurrection, not to other than Us, so We will then recompense them according to their deeds. And the use of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), ﴿raji'un﴾, serves to indicate permanence and certainty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteous deeds﴾ and so on, is an elaboration of the recompense, meaning: whoever does some of the righteous deeds, or some portion of the righteous deeds, ﴿while he is a believer﴾ in Allah and His messengers, ﴿there will be no denial (kufran) of his striving﴾, meaning: there will be no deprivation of the reward for that deed of his. He expressed this by kufran, which is the concealing of a blessing and denying it, in order to show the complete exoneration of Him, exalted is He, from it, by depicting it in the form of what is impossible for Him, exalted is He, to commit of ugly acts, and by presenting the reward in the context of matters that are obligatory upon Him, exalted is He. He used the negation of the genus (nafy al-jins) for emphasis in declaring Him free of such things, and He expressed the deed by striving (sa'y) to show the importance attached to it.

﴿And indeed We are, for it﴾, meaning: for his striving, ﴿recording (katibun)﴾, meaning: inscribing it in the records of their deeds, not leaving out anything of that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 95:

﴿And it is forbidden for a town﴾ — that is, it is impossible (mumtani') for its people, and it is inconceivable (ghayr mutasawwar) that it should come from them. It is read as "hirm," which is a dialect form like "hill" and "halal" (ḥill and ḥalāl, both meaning "lawful").

﴿We destroyed them﴾ — We decreed their destruction, or Our judgement of it, because of the extreme of their transgression and obstinacy.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿that they will not return﴾ — it is in the position of the nominative (raf') in that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "forbidden," or it is an agent (fa'il) of it that takes the place of its predicate. The clause serves to confirm the content of what precedes it, namely His saying: ﴿Every one of them will be brought back to Us﴾. What is conveyed by "anna" of affirmation (tahqiq) is considered in the negation derived from "forbidden," not in the negated element; that is, it is absolutely impossible that they fail to return to Us for recompense, not that their actual non-return is impossible. The specific mention of the impossibility of the non-return of [the people of] the town, although the impossibility extends to the non-return of all, as expressed by His saying: ﴿Every one of them will be brought back to Us﴾, is because they are the ones who deny resurrection and return, and no others. It was also said: their return to repentance is impossible, with "la" being superfluous (silah). It is read as "innahum la yarji'un" with a kasra, as a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf ta'lili) for what precedes it; so "forbidden" is the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: "forbidden for it is that," namely what was mentioned in the previous verse of righteous deeds accompanied by faith and appreciated effort. Then it gives the reason with His saying: ﴿that they do not return﴾ from the disbelief they are upon — so how would that not be impossible? It is also permissible to read the fathah form in this sense too, by deleting the lam from it, meaning: "because they do not return."

"And "until" in His saying, ﴿until when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾, etc., is the "until" after which speech is related. According to the first view, it is an end-point (ghayah) for what the preceding words indicate, as if it were said: they will continue in the destruction they are in, until, when the Resurrection comes, they will return to Us and say: ﴿"Woe to us!"﴾ ... etc. According to the second view, it is an end-point for the prohibition, meaning: the prevention of their return to repentance continues until, when the Resurrection comes, they will return to it at a time when repentance will not benefit them. According to the third view, it is an end-point for the non-return from disbelief, meaning: they do not return from it until, when the Resurrection comes, they will return from it at a time when returning will not benefit them.

Gog and Magog (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj) are two tribes of mankind. It has been said: people are ten parts, nine of which are Gog and Magog. The meaning of their "opening" is the opening of their barrier, by omitting the mudaf (the governed noun) and placing the mudaf ilayhi (the governing noun) in its position. It has also been read as "fattahat" with the doubled letter.

﴿And they﴾, i.e., Gog and Magog; it has been said: mankind, ﴿from every slope﴾, i.e., elevation of the earth. It has been read as "jadath," which is the grave. ﴿They will swarm﴾, i.e., they will hasten. Its origin is approaching steps together with haste. It has been read with a damma on the sin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 21, verse 97:

﴿And the true promise draws near﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "futiḥat" (it is opened), and what is meant by it is what comes after the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya) of resurrection, reckoning and recompense, not the first blast.

﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾ is the answer to the conditional, and "idha" (then, suddenly) is for sudden occurrence (li-l-mufaja'a), standing in place of the consequential fa' (fa' al-jaza'iyya), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then, behold, they despair﴾. When the fa' enters upon it, it reinforces the connection of the consequent to the condition. The pronoun (al-damir) refers to the matter (li-l-qissa), or it is an ambiguous pronoun explained by what follows it.

﴿Woe to us!﴾ is in the sense of an implied saying (qawl muqaddar) that occurred as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), meaning: they say, "Woe to us! This is the day of your presence," or it is said that it is the answer to the conditional. ﴿We were indeed in complete heedlessness (ghafla tamma)﴾ ﴿of this﴾, which overtook us, of resurrection and of returning to Him, exalted is He, for recompense, and we did not know that it was true. ﴿Rather, we were wrongdoers﴾ is a turning away (idrab) from what preceded it, namely the description of themselves as heedless. That is: we were not heedless of it, since it was pointed out to us by the signs and warnings, but rather we were wrongdoers by means of those signs and warnings, denying them; or we were wrongdoers to our own selves by exposing them to the everlasting punishment through denial.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are the fuel of Hell﴾ is an address to the disbelievers of Makkah and an explicit statement of the outcome of their affair, even though it was already known in general terms from what preceded it. It is meant as an exaggeration in warning and as a removal of excuses.

﴿And what you worship﴾ is an expression for their idols, because they are what they worship, as the word "ma" makes clear. It has been narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the verse, Ibn al-Za'abari said to him: "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah! Are not the Jews those who worshipped 'Uzayr, the Christians those who worshipped the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh those who worshipped the angels?" He (ﷺ) replied: "How ignorant you are of the language of your people! Did you not understand that 'ma' is for what does not reason?" It is not contradicted by what is narrated that he (ﷺ) answered him by saying, "Rather, they worshipped the devils who commanded them to do so," nor by what is narrated that Ibn al-Za'abari said, "This is specific to our gods, or to everything that is worshipped besides Allah," and he (ﷺ) said, "Rather, it is for everything that is worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted."
